pathways.name: chromatin organization
pathways.pathway_description: The assembly or remodeling of chromatin composed of DNA complexed with histones, other associated proteins, and sometimes RNA. [PMID:20404130]
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: Chromatin organization pathways regulate how DNA is packaged and accessed, and their disruption can alter large gene expression programs relevant to neurodevelopmental timing, neuronal differentiation, and cortical circuit formation in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The cited ASD studies implicating chromatin regulators (e.g., CHD8, CREBBP, BAZ2B, ASH1L) support a model in which global transcriptional dysregulation, rather than single-gene effects, contributes to ASD pathology.
Intersection-gene interpretation: The intersection genes ACTB, ACTL6B, ARID1A, ARID1B, and ARID2 encode core structural and remodeling components of chromatin-associated complexes, suggesting that ASD risk may converge on ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling and actin-based nuclear architecture. ARID1B in particular is directly linked to ASD and neuropathology, indicating that perturbation of SWI/SNF (BAF) complex function can disrupt neuronal gene expression programs critical for social and cognitive development.
PubMed literature synthesis: ASD neuropathology and animal model work implicating ARID1B and CHD8, together with reports of CREBBP and ASH1L mutations in ASD cohorts, collectively support chromatin remodeling and histone modification as recurrent mechanistic themes in ASD. Studies of altered cortical complexity in autism and CHD8 genomic targets further indicate that chromatin organization defects can reshape cortical development and transcriptional networks in ASD brains.
Cell/tissue context: The literature emphasizes cortical tissue and brain neuropathology, indicating that chromatin organization defects act prominently in developing and mature cerebral cortex. Placental studies involving CREBBP also suggest that chromatin-related mechanisms may extend to extra-embryonic tissues relevant to prenatal ASD risk. [PMID:30692911] [PMID:34356069] [PMID:39763008]

paragraphs: 111 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in chromatin organization (GO:0006325).

Several core chromatin remodelers in this pathway have direct and well-documented links to autism spectrum disorder. CHD8 encodes an ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler that regulates transcription by repositioning nucleosomes, and multiple human genetic studies identify recurrent de novo loss-of-function variants in CHD8 in individuals with autism spectrum disorder, often accompanied by macrocephaly and intellectual disability; comparative work across CHD8 haploinsufficient models has highlighted shared genomic targets despite model-specific transcriptional effects. ARID1B and ARID1A encode DNA-binding subunits of SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complexes, and neuropathological and animal model data implicate ARID1B in abnormal cortical development and autism spectrum disorder-related behaviors, supporting a broader role of SWI/SNF dysfunction in neurodevelopmental phenotypes. ASH1L encodes a histone methyltransferase that deposits activating methyl marks on histone H3 tails, and de novo disruptive variants in ASH1L have been reported in individuals with autism spectrum disorder, indicating that disruption of this activator of gene expression contributes to disease liability.

Other histone- and chromatin-binding factors in the enriched set reinforce the centrality of epigenetic regulation in autism spectrum disorder. BAZ2B encodes a bromodomain-containing chromatin reader that binds acetylated histones and participates in nucleosome remodeling complexes, and haploinsufficiency of BAZ2B has been described as a cause of developmental delay, intellectual disability, and autism spectrum disorder, providing a direct genotype–phenotype link. CREBBP encodes a transcriptional coactivator and histone acetyltransferase that acetylates lysine residues on histone tails to open chromatin; structural and sequence variants affecting CREBBP have been observed in autism spectrum disorder cohorts, including in long-read sequencing studies of complex duplications, and CREBBP emerges in placental transcriptomic analyses that explore regulatory RNA networks in autism spectrum disorder. The linker histone gene H1-4, a component of higher-order chromatin compaction, is closely related to HIST1H1E, and an autism spectrum disorder case with mutation in a H1 linker histone has been reported in the epigenetics literature, underscoring that perturbation of linker histone function and chromatin fiber architecture can contribute to autism spectrum disorder.

The remaining genes enriched in chromatin organization can be grouped into functional clusters that together define a broad perturbation of epigenomic control in autism spectrum disorder. A chromatin remodeling cluster includes ATRX, BICRA, CHD1, CHD2, CHD3, CHD4, CHD7, ARID2, and KANSL1, which encode ATP-dependent remodelers and associated factors that reposition or exchange nucleosomes and help establish regional chromatin states in the developing brain. A histone modification cluster comprises writers such as DNMT3A, DOT1L, EHMT1, EP300, KAT6A, KMT2A, KMT2C, KMT2E, KMT5B, and MSL3, erasers including HDAC4, HDAC8, KDM2B, KDM3B, KDM5B, KDM5C, and KDM6B, and histone substrates H3-3B, H4C11, H4C3, and H4C5, reflecting coordinated disruption of DNA methylation and histone methylation and acetylation dynamics. A chromatin-binding and architectural cluster includes CBX1, CTCF, MECP2, HCFC1, BCORL1, NIPBL, and BAZ2B, which bind modified histones or DNA and contribute to higher-order chromatin insulation and long-range regulation. A transcriptional and RNA-processing cluster comprising CTR9, HNRNPK, HNRNPU, DDX23, and DHX9 links chromatin state to transcription elongation and RNA metabolism. A signaling and kinase cluster including BRAF, BRSK2, CSNK1G1, CSNK2A1, DYRK1A, MTOR, and CASK connects extracellular and intracellular signaling to chromatin regulatory machinery, while structural and cytoskeletal components such as ACTB and ACTL6B function within remodeling complexes and nuclear architecture. NCOA1 serves as a nuclear receptor coactivator that bridges signaling to chromatin modification, and HUWE1 functions as an E3 ligase that regulates the stability of chromatin regulators, further integrating these clusters into a coherent chromatin organization network.

Chromatin organization therefore emerges as a major axis through which genetic risk converges in autism spectrum disorder, with enrichment of genes that collectively regulate nucleosome positioning, histone modification, and higher-order genome architecture in developing neural tissues. The principal driver genes are CHD8, ARID1B, ASH1L, BAZ2B, and CREBBP, which have direct genetic or functional evidence linking disruptive variants to autism spectrum disorder, developmental delay, or characteristic neuropathology. Well-documented interactions between intersection genes include the participation of CHD8, ARID1B, ARID1A, and BICRA in SWI/SNF-like chromatin remodeling assemblies and the cooperative action of CREBBP, EP300, and KAT6A as histone acetyltransferases that create binding sites for bromodomain-containing readers such as BAZ2B. The convergence of these interacting chromatin regulators supports a model in which disruption of epigenomic programming is a central contributor to autism spectrum disorder pathogenesis in this gene set.

pathways.name: neuron projection development
pathways.pathway_description: The process whose specific outcome is the progression of a neuron projection over time, from its formation to the mature structure. A neuron projection is any process extending from a neural cell, such as axons or dendrites (collectively called neurites). [GOC:mah]
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: The neuron projection development pathway indicates that disrupted formation and maturation of axons and dendrites is a central mechanism in ASD, leading to miswired neural circuits and altered connectivity. Such defects can manifest as abnormal long-range and local projections, consistent with connectomic findings in ASD.
Intersection-gene interpretation: ACTB and ACTL6B influence cytoskeletal dynamics and chromatin state, respectively, thereby affecting the structural and transcriptional programs required for neurite outgrowth, while ADNP and ARX regulate neurodevelopmental gene expression programs that guide projection patterning. ANK3 contributes to the organization of the axon initial segment and may influence the maturation and functional polarization of neuronal projections, linking structural development to excitability.
PubMed literature synthesis: Pathway-level studies of Chd8 haploinsufficiency and single-cell methylation profiling in ASD prefrontal cortex show that ASD risk converges on transcriptional and epigenetic programs controlling cortical neuron development, including projection formation. Gene-level ASD evidence for CNTNAP2, DSCAM, FMR1, and CDKL5—each known to regulate neurite outgrowth, synapse formation, or cortical circuit assembly—supports a model in which genetic risk perturbs neuron projection development, leading to ASD-relevant circuit dysfunction.
Cell/tissue context: The evidence supports involvement of developing cortical projection neurons, particularly in the prefrontal cortex where Chd8-dependent transcriptional dysregulation and ASD-associated methylation signatures have been observed. [PMID:40967226] [PMID:39185167] [PMID:42320469]

paragraphs: 81 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in neuron projection development (GO:0031175).

Among the cytoskeletal regulators enriched in this pathway, ACTB and MACF1 illustrate how perturbations of the physical scaffold of neurites may contribute to ASD. ACTB encodes β-actin, the core component of filamentous actin that drives growth cone motility, filopodial dynamics and dendritic spine morphogenesis; recurrent ACTB variants have been reported in patients with developmental delay and autistic features, and experimental disruption of β-actin dynamics impairs neurite outgrowth and branching. MACF1 encodes a spectraplakin that coordinates microtubule and actin networks along axons and dendrites, and loss-of-function of MACF1 in neuronal models causes defective axon extension and pathfinding, a cellular phenotype that mirrors the disrupted long-range connectivity consistently described in ASD neuropathology.

Several synaptic organizer genes in this pathway provide a direct link between neuron projection development and clinically defined ASD. CNTNAP2 encodes a neurexin family cell-adhesion molecule concentrated at the axon initial segment and nodes of Ranvier; rare homozygous and heterozygous CNTNAP2 mutations produce syndromic forms of ASD with language delay and seizures, and CNTNAP2 dysfunction in animal models leads to abnormal neurite arborization and cortical connectivity. DSCAM encodes a cell-adhesion molecule critical for self-avoidance and laminar targeting of axons and dendrites, and recurrent DSCAM variants have been identified in individuals with ASD and intellectual disability, consistent with its established role in tiling and spacing of neurites. FMR1, which encodes an RNA-binding protein that represses translation of many synaptic mRNAs, is the causative gene for fragile X syndrome, the most common monogenic cause of ASD; FMR1 deficiency leads to excessive, immature dendritic spines on cortical pyramidal neurons, directly implicating dysregulated dendritic morphogenesis in ASD pathogenesis.

Additional synaptic signaling components enriched in neuron projection development further connect projection morphology with functional synapse maturation. DLG4 encodes a postsynaptic scaffold that anchors glutamate receptors at excitatory synapses; DLG4 disruption in neuronal models causes altered dendritic spine density and impaired synaptic plasticity, phenotypes that parallel the dendritic abnormalities described in ASD cortical tissue. NLGN3 and NRXN1 encode complementary postsynaptic and presynaptic adhesion molecules, respectively, that form trans-synaptic complexes essential for synapse formation along developing axons and dendrites; rare disruptive variants in both NLGN3 and NRXN1 have been repeatedly observed in ASD cohorts, and experimental manipulation of these genes alters synapse number and dendritic arbor complexity. RELN encodes an extracellular matrix protein that guides neuronal migration and layer-specific targeting of axons and dendrites; reduced RELN expression has been described in ASD cortex, and RELN perturbation in model systems results in misplaced projection neurons and aberrant dendritic orientation.

The enriched gene set also includes regulators of axonal transport and growth cone guidance that are required to elaborate functional neuron projections. KIF1A and KIF5C encode kinesin motors that drive anterograde transport of synaptic vesicle precursors and organelles along axons and dendrites; pathogenic KIF1A and KIF5C variants cause neurodevelopmental syndromes with spasticity, intellectual disability and autistic behaviors, consistent with defective cargo delivery to growing neurites. BRAF, a serine/threonine kinase in the MAPK cascade, lies upstream of multiple neurite outgrowth pathways, and BRAF mutations produce developmental syndromes frequently accompanied by ASD, in which altered MAPK signaling is associated with abnormal dendritic arborization in experimental models. PTEN and PTPN11 encode regulators of PI3K–AKT and MAPK signaling, respectively, both of which control neuronal size and axon growth; germline PTEN mutations are enriched in ASD individuals with macrocephaly, and PTPN11 mutations cause syndromes with increased ASD prevalence, supporting a role for dysregulated growth signaling in projection development defects.

Beyond these individually well-characterized genes, the remaining intersection genes can be organized into functional clusters that together support neuron projection development. A synaptic scaffolding and signaling cluster (CAMK2A, CAMK2B, PPP3CA, PPP1R9B, NCKAP1, BRSK2, MAPK8IP3, MYCBP2, LRRC4C, NLGN2, NRXN3, NTNG1, NTNG2) modulates activity-dependent remodeling and adhesion along developing neurites. A transcriptional and chromatin-regulatory cluster (ADNP, ARX, BCL11A, CUX2, EP300, FOXG1, FRYL, MECP2, MEF2C, NFIB, NR2F1, NR4A2, PAX6) establishes neuronal subtype identity and projection patterns by controlling expression of cytoskeletal and guidance genes. A guidance and adhesion cluster (ANK3, CTNNA2, CTNNB1, CNTNAP2, DSCAM, DMD, GFAP, LRRC4C, NTRK2, PTK7, RELN) regulates axon initial segment assembly, neurite fasciculation and responsiveness to extracellular cues. Finally, a vesicle trafficking and membrane dynamics cluster (ATP9A, CAPRIN1, DLG4, HERC1, KIF1A, KIF5C, NOVA2, NRXN1, NRXN3, PRKD1, PAK1) supports polarized delivery of receptors and adhesion molecules to tips of extending axons and dendrites.

Neuron projection development emerges from this analysis as a central developmental process through which ASD risk genes converge, with alterations in dendritic and axonal growth, guidance and synapse formation providing a cellular substrate for the atypical connectivity observed in ASD brains. The principal driver genes are CNTNAP2, FMR1 and PTEN, which each carry strong human genetic evidence for ASD and exert direct control over neurite arborization, spine maturation and neuronal growth. Well-documented interactions between intersection genes, such as the trans-synaptic pairing of NRXN1 and NLGN3 and the postsynaptic scaffolding role of DLG4 in stabilizing synapses downstream of these adhesion complexes, illustrate how combined perturbation of multiple components within this pathway may amplify projection-level defects. Disruption of neuron projection development therefore represents a plausible mechanistic axis that links diverse molecular lesions to shared neuroanatomical and behavioral phenotypes in ASD.

pathways.name: regulation of synaptic plasticity
pathways.pathway_description: A process that modulates synaptic plasticity, the ability of synapses to change as circumstances require. They may alter function, such as increasing or decreasing their sensitivity, or they may increase or decrease in actual numbers. [GOC:dph, GOC:jid, GOC:tb, PMID:11891290]
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: This pathway encompasses mechanisms that modulate synaptic plasticity, a core process for learning and circuit refinement, and dysregulated plasticity is a central mechanistic hypothesis for ASD. Perturbations in regulators of plasticity can impair experience-dependent tuning of neural circuits, contributing to the cognitive, social, and sensory features of ASD.
Intersection-gene interpretation: CAMK2A, CAMK2B, and CAMK2D encode CaMKII isoforms that are key activity-dependent regulators of synaptic strength, so their involvement in this pathway directly links calcium signaling to plasticity changes relevant to ASD. BRAF and DLG4 (PSD-95) participate in signaling and scaffolding at excitatory synapses, and altered function of these regulators would be expected to disrupt the induction and maintenance of synaptic plasticity in ASD-relevant circuits.
PubMed literature synthesis: Reviews on microglia at the tripartite synapse and transcriptional studies implicating altered Wnt signaling in ASD and Phelan-McDermid syndrome converge on the idea that synaptic plasticity is modulated not only by neuronal genes (e.g., SHANK3, SYNGAP1, MECP2, STXBP1) but also by glial and developmental signaling pathways. Neuropathology and animal model work, together with ASD associations in NF1, further support that diverse ASD genes converge on pathways that regulate synaptic plasticity rather than a single receptor or channel.
Cell/tissue context: The evidence supports a context of excitatory synapses in the brain, particularly cortical circuits where DLG4, CaMKII isoforms, SHANK3, and SYNGAP1 are prominent, and includes microglia at tripartite synapses as additional cellular players in plasticity regulation. [PMID:38132147] [PMID:36756634] [PMID:32560742]

paragraphs: 31 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in regulation of synaptic plasticity (GO:0048167).

Among the intersection genes, SHANK3, SYNGAP1 and GRIN2B stand out as core regulators of glutamatergic synaptic plasticity with strong human genetic support in ASD. SHANK3 encodes a postsynaptic scaffold at excitatory synapses, and disruptive mutations in SHANK3 are established causes of syndromic and non-syndromic ASD, with clinical cohorts reporting ASD or ASD-like social-communication deficits in a substantial proportion of individuals carrying SHANK3 haploinsufficiency. SYNGAP1 encodes a Ras-GAP localized to the postsynaptic density, and truncating SYNGAP1 mutations are repeatedly identified in ASD and intellectual disability cohorts, where they are associated with global developmental delay and seizures, supporting a role for disturbed postsynaptic signaling in ASD. GRIN2B encodes an NMDA receptor subunit that helps govern calcium permeability and plasticity thresholds, and ASD neuropathology studies include GRIN2B among recurrently disrupted genes, linking altered NMDA receptor composition to ASD-related phenotypes.

MECP2, FMR1 and NF1 further connect regulation of synaptic plasticity to syndromic forms of ASD with characteristic clinical presentations. MECP2 encodes a methyl-CpG binding protein, and ASD cohort sequencing studies report pathogenic MECP2 variants among affected individuals, in keeping with the high rates of autistic features observed in disorders caused by MECP2 dysfunction. FMR1 encodes an RNA-binding protein whose loss causes fragile X syndrome, and ASD neuropathology analyses explicitly highlight FMR1 as an ASD-associated gene, consistent with the high prevalence of ASD diagnoses among individuals with FMR1 expansions. NF1 encodes a Ras-GAP that modulates Ras–MAPK signaling, and a dedicated clinical study of children with neurofibromatosis type 1 reports ASD within an unselected NF1 cohort, indicating that dysregulated Ras signaling and its impact on synaptic plasticity are directly relevant to ASD.

STXBP1, NTRK2 and BRAF illustrate how presynaptic release machinery and neurotrophic signaling converge on plasticity mechanisms implicated in ASD. STXBP1 encodes a key component of the synaptic vesicle release apparatus, and de novo STXBP1 mutations have been identified in ASD cohorts, where they are associated with early-onset epilepsy and developmental delay, pointing to impaired presynaptic regulation of plasticity. NTRK2 encodes the receptor for a major neurotrophic factor that supports activity-dependent synaptic strengthening and maturation, positioning it as a modulator of structural and functional plasticity. BRAF, already noted in earlier pathways in this report, functions here as a central kinase within MAPK cascades that translate synaptic activity and growth factor signals into transcriptional programs, thereby influencing long-term forms of synaptic plasticity relevant to ASD.

The remaining genes enriched in regulation of synaptic plasticity can be organized into functional clusters. A postsynaptic scaffold and receptor complex cluster includes DLG4, SHANK2, GRIN1, GRIN2A, GRIA3 and PPFIA3, which together shape the architecture and signaling properties of excitatory synapses. A calcium and kinase signaling cluster, comprising CAMK2A, CAMK2B, CAMK2D, MEF2C and YWHAG, transduces activity-dependent calcium influx into phosphorylation events and transcriptional responses that modulate synaptic strength. A membrane excitability and vesicle cycle cluster includes KCNB1, KCNQ3, VAMP2 and STXBP1, which regulate action potential firing and neurotransmitter release dynamics. A chromatin and transcriptional regulation cluster involving KMT2A, MECP2 and UBE3A links synaptic activity to longer-term changes in gene expression and protein turnover that stabilize plasticity. A structural and guidance cluster comprising MAP1A, RELN, IQSEC2, TSHZ3 and GFAP influences dendritic architecture, synapse formation and the cellular milieu in which plasticity occurs.

Regulation of synaptic plasticity thus emerges as a major axis through which ASD risk genes converge, with disturbances in postsynaptic scaffolding, NMDA receptor composition, Ras–MAPK signaling and presynaptic release all capable of shifting the thresholds and stability of synaptic change. The principal driver genes are SHANK3, SYNGAP1, GRIN2B, MECP2, FMR1 and NF1, which collectively anchor the link between this pathway and ASD through recurrent pathogenic variants and well-characterized clinical phenotypes. Documented interactions among the intersection genes, such as the known functional association between SHANK3 and DLG4 within the postsynaptic density, provide a structural substrate for coordinated disruption of plasticity mechanisms in ASD. This enrichment supports a model in which altered regulation of synaptic plasticity is a central biological process underlying a substantial subset of ASD cases represented in the gene list used for this analysis.

pathways.name: modulation of excitatory postsynaptic potential
pathways.pathway_description: Any process that modulates the frequency, rate or extent of excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP). EPSP is a process that leads to a temporary increase in postsynaptic potential due to the flow of positively charged ions into the postsynaptic cell. The flow of ions that causes an EPSP is an excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC) and makes it easier for the neuron to fire an action potential. [GOC:dos]
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: This pathway captures processes that alter the strength or dynamics of excitatory postsynaptic potentials, directly reflecting control of synaptic excitation. In ASD, altered modulation of EPSPs provides a mechanistic substrate for the widely observed imbalance between excitation and inhibition and for abnormal information processing in cortical and other brain circuits.
Intersection-gene interpretation: GRIN1 encodes an essential NMDA receptor subunit whose function critically shapes EPSP amplitude and plasticity, so its perturbation can directly alter excitatory synaptic responses in ASD-relevant circuits. CELF4, CUX2, DLG4, and DMPK influence RNA processing, transcriptional regulation, postsynaptic scaffolding, and signaling at excitatory synapses, indicating that both receptor function and synaptic organization contribute to EPSP modulation.
PubMed literature synthesis: ASD literature emphasizing synaptic genes such as SHANK3, NRXN1, NLGN3, and GRIN2B, together with PTEN-regulated splicing of ASD-associated transcripts, supports a model in which altered postsynaptic receptor composition and scaffolding disrupt EPSP properties. These findings align with the present pathway, suggesting that convergent genetic perturbations in synaptic components and regulators ultimately manifest as abnormal EPSP modulation in ASD.
Cell/tissue context: The evidence supports involvement of excitatory glutamatergic synapses in neurons, particularly within cortical and cerebellar circuits where EPSP modulation is critical for information processing and plasticity.

paragraphs: 17 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in modulation of excitatory postsynaptic potential (GO:0098815).

Several of the best-characterized autism spectrum disorder genes in this pathway encode glutamatergic postsynaptic scaffolding and receptor components that directly shape excitatory postsynaptic potentials. SHANK3 encodes a core postsynaptic density scaffold at excitatory synapses that organizes glutamate receptors and signaling complexes; multiple studies have established that heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or small deletions in SHANK3 lead to autism spectrum disorder with frequent intellectual disability and language impairment, and recurrent microdeletions at this locus account for a measurable subset of syndromic autism spectrum disorder cases. GRIN2B, GRIN2A, and GRIN1 encode subunits of NMDA-type glutamate receptors, which conduct the cation influx that underlies excitatory postsynaptic currents and thus determine both amplitude and kinetics of excitatory postsynaptic potentials; rare disruptive variants in GRIN2B have been repeatedly reported in autism spectrum disorder cohorts, and animal models reviewed in the autism spectrum disorder literature support a role for GRIN2B perturbation in social and cognitive phenotypes that parallel human disease. Together, variation in these scaffolding and receptor genes provides direct genetic support for altered NMDA receptor-mediated modulation of excitatory postsynaptic potential in autism spectrum disorder.

Cell-adhesion molecules at excitatory synapses further modulate excitatory postsynaptic potentials by governing synapse formation, alignment, and stability. NLGN3 encodes a postsynaptic neuroligin that binds presynaptic neurexins; rare missense and truncating variants in NLGN3 have been reported in individuals with autism spectrum disorder, and reviews of neuropathology and animal models highlight that perturbation of NLGN3 alters excitatory synaptic transmission and social behavior in vivo. NRXN1 encodes a presynaptic neurexin that interacts with neuroligins to align active zones and postsynaptic receptor fields, thereby influencing the probability and synchrony of excitatory neurotransmission; recurrent heterozygous NRXN1 deletions have been identified in autism spectrum disorder, and animal work summarized in the autism spectrum disorder literature ties NRXN1 disruption to impaired excitatory synapse function. NLGN2 and NLGN4X are additional neuroligin genes enriched in this pathway whose synaptic adhesion roles are consistent with a broader neuroligin–neurexin gene list contributing to the modulation of excitatory postsynaptic potential in autism spectrum disorder, even though direct disease-gene references were not attached for them here.

PTEN represents a mechanistically distinct but convergent modulator of excitatory postsynaptic responses. PTEN is a lipid and protein phosphatase that constrains PI3K–AKT–mTOR signaling and thereby regulates neuronal growth, dendritic arborization, and synaptic structure, all of which influence the integration of excitatory inputs. Autism spectrum disorder-focused studies have shown that PTEN controls alternative splicing of autism spectrum disorder-associated transcripts in primary neurons and that PTEN variants interact with genetic background to modify cerebellar neuronal differentiation, indicating that PTEN dysfunction can reshape neuronal morphology and gene expression programs in ways that alter excitatory synaptic function. Clinically, germline PTEN mutations are found in a subset of individuals with autism spectrum disorder, often in the context of macrocephaly, supporting PTEN as a major contributor to altered excitatory circuit properties that impact excitatory postsynaptic potential modulation.

The remaining genes enriched in this term fall into three functional clusters that converge on modulation of excitatory postsynaptic potential. A synaptic scaffolding and active zone cluster includes DLG4, RIMS1, and RIMS2: DLG4 encodes a postsynaptic density scaffold that couples glutamate receptors to intracellular signaling complexes, while RIMS1 and RIMS2 encode presynaptic active zone organizers that regulate vesicle priming and release probability; coordinated presynaptic and postsynaptic scaffolding directly shapes the size and reliability of excitatory postsynaptic currents. A synaptic regulatory and splicing cluster encompasses CELF4, DMPK, and ZMYND8: CELF4 encodes an RNA-binding protein that modulates neuronal mRNA processing and translation, DMPK participates in kinase signaling with documented effects on RNA metabolism and cellular architecture, and ZMYND8 acts as a chromatin-associated regulator; by altering expression and processing of synaptic genes, this cluster can indirectly tune the molecular determinants of excitatory postsynaptic potential. A cortical and laminar organization cluster comprises CUX2 and RELN: CUX2 encodes a transcription factor enriched in cortical projection neurons, and RELN encodes a secreted signal critical for neuronal migration and synaptic maturation; altered cortical layering and synapse development in this cluster would be expected to change the number, distribution, and efficacy of excitatory synapses and thus the summation of excitatory postsynaptic potentials.

Modulation of excitatory postsynaptic potential emerges from this pathway as a central synaptic process through which diverse autism spectrum disorder genes converge to influence neuronal signaling. The principal driver genes are SHANK3, GRIN2B, PTEN, NLGN3, and NRXN1, which have both strong autism spectrum disorder genetic evidence and direct mechanistic links to excitatory synaptic transmission. Physical and functional interactions between several of the genes listed for this record, particularly the neuroligin–neurexin pair NLGN3–NRXN1 and the scaffold–receptor partnership of DLG4 with NMDA receptor subunits such as GRIN1 and GRIN2B, highlight that multiple components of shared synaptic complexes are affected. Disruption within this network is likely to alter the amplitude, timing, and plasticity of excitatory postsynaptic potentials in developing and mature circuits, providing a biologically coherent route from gene-level perturbation to the excitatory–inhibitory imbalance and atypical circuit dynamics characteristic of autism spectrum disorder.

pathways.name: histone methyltransferase activity
pathways.pathway_description: Catalysis of the reaction: S-adenosyl-L-methionine + histone = S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine + methyl-histone. Histone methylation generally occurs on either an arginine or a lysine residue. [GOC:curators]
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: Histone methyltransferase activity modulates chromatin state and gene expression, and its disruption can broadly alter neurodevelopmental transcriptional programs relevant to ASD. Multiple ASD-associated histone methyltransferases suggest that epigenetic misregulation is a recurrent mechanistic axis in ASD.
Intersection-gene interpretation: The intersection genes ASH1L, DOT1L, EHMT1, KMT2A, and KMT2C encode histone methyltransferases that deposit activating or repressive methyl marks, thereby shaping neuronal gene expression landscapes. ASH1L and KMT2C, both directly linked to ASD, indicate that perturbation of H3K4/H3K36 methylation-dependent activation of developmental genes is a specific route to ASD risk.
PubMed literature synthesis: ASD cohort and family studies implicating ASH1L, KMT2C, NSD1, and SETD1B, along with disease-similarity network analyses, collectively support a strong association between histone methyltransferase gene disruption and ASD. These findings reinforce a model in which convergent defects in histone methylation pathways underlie shared neurodevelopmental and cognitive phenotypes across ASD cases.
Cell/tissue context: The available evidence points to histone methyltransferase function in the developing nervous system, but specific brain regions or cell types are not resolved from the supplied pathway-level evidence. paragraphs: 15 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in histone methyltransferase activity (GO:0042054).

Among the lysine-directed histone methyltransferases in the intersection, ASH1L, KMT2C and SETD1B stand out because of direct ASD genetic evidence. ASH1L encodes a SET domain histone methyltransferase that deposits activating methyl marks on histones, and multiple studies have identified both de novo and inherited ASH1L variants in individuals with ASD, including families with recurrence across three affected siblings, supporting a contribution of ASH1L-mediated histone methylation to familial ASD risk. KMT2C, another large SET domain methyltransferase that targets lysine residues on histone H3, has likewise been implicated in multiplex ASD families, where inherited KMT2C variants co-segregate with ASD in the presence of additional risk alleles, pointing to a polygenic architecture that converges on histone methylation. SETD1B encodes an H3K4 methyltransferase; exome sequencing in ancestrally diverse ASD cohorts has identified SETD1B variants among affected individuals, indicating that disruption of SETD1B-dependent H3K4 methylation is a recurrent feature across ASD populations rather than being confined to a single ancestry group.

NSD1 provides further support that dysregulated histone methyltransferase activity is directly involved in ASD. NSD1 encodes a histone methyltransferase that catalyzes methylation of lysine residues within histone H3, and a clinical report has described an NSD1 variant in a child diagnosed with ASD in conjunction with congenital heart disease, linking pathogenic alteration of NSD1 catalytic activity to a syndromic ASD presentation. The convergence of ASH1L, KMT2C, SETD1B and NSD1 within this enriched term indicates that multiple, independently validated ASD genes encode histone methyltransferases whose dysfunction is compatible with core ASD phenotypes, sometimes accompanied by additional congenital anomalies.

The remaining genes can be organized into functional clusters reflecting distinct components of histone methylation machinery. A first cluster comprises additional SET domain lysine methyltransferases involved in writing diverse histone marks, including DOT1L, EHMT1, KMT2A, KMT5B, NSD2, SETD1A, SETD2 and SETD5, which together broaden the range of potentially affected histone lysine residues and methylation states beyond those linked to ASH1L, KMT2C, SETD1B and NSD1. A second cluster contains PRMT9, which provides arginine-directed histone methyltransferase activity that complements the lysine-specific enzymes, extending the enrichment to arginine as well as lysine substrates. A third cluster centers on WDR5 and SETBP1, which act as core complex components or cofactors within histone methyltransferase assemblies rather than as catalytic enzymes themselves; their presence in this term underscores that both catalytic and scaffolding elements of methyltransferase complexes are represented among ASD-associated genes.

The histone methyltransferase activity pathway therefore highlights a coherent axis of ASD risk genes whose shared biochemical role is to install methyl marks on histone tails, with the principal driver genes being ASH1L, KMT2C, SETD1B and NSD1, each supported by direct ASD genetic data. Variation in these genes, together with additional lysine and arginine methyltransferases and their cofactors in the intersection, indicates that altered patterns of histone methylation constitute a recurrent molecular theme in ASD. WDR5 and multiple SET domain genes are known to assemble into multi-subunit histone methyltransferase complexes, providing a mechanistic context in which variants in different intersection genes can converge on the same chromatin-modifying machinery. This enrichment supports a model in which disruption of histone methyltransferase activity, through both catalytic subunits and associated factors, contributes materially to ASD pathogenesis.

pathways.name: ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler activity
pathways.pathway_description: An activity, driven by ATP hydrolysis, that modulates the contacts between histones and DNA, resulting in a change in chromosome architecture within the nucleosomal array, leading to chromatin remodeling. [PMID:14729263, PMID:19165147, PMID:21862382, PMID:30867599, PMID:34313222]
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: The ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler activity pathway implicates epigenetic dysregulation of gene expression programs as a mechanistic contributor to ASD, by altering chromatin accessibility at neurodevelopmental loci. Such remodeling defects can broadly impact neuronal differentiation, synapse formation, and circuit maturation.
Intersection-gene interpretation: CHD1, CHD2, CHD3, CHD4, and CHD7 are ATP-dependent chromatin remodelers that reposition nucleosomes and modulate histone–DNA contacts, thereby controlling transcriptional programs essential for brain development and neuronal function; their disruption could lead to widespread misexpression of ASD-relevant genes. Overlap with CHD8-associated disease literature suggests that these CHD family members participate in shared chromatin-remodeling networks whose perturbation can converge on ASD phenotypes.
PubMed literature synthesis: Disease-gene studies of CHD1, CHD2, CHD4, and CHD7 in epilepsy, together with multiple reports of CHD8 variants and CHD8–Notch pathway interactions in ASD, indicate that CHD-family chromatin remodelers are critical regulators of neurodevelopmental gene networks whose disruption can produce ASD and related neurodevelopmental phenotypes. Rescue of CHD8 suppression phenotypes by SINEUP RNA further supports a causal role for impaired chromatin remodeling in ASD-like molecular and cellular abnormalities.

paragraphs: 9 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler activity (GO:0140658).

Among the intersection genes, CHD8 stands out as a well-characterized ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler in ASD. CHD8 encodes a chromodomain helicase DNA-binding ATPase that directly utilizes ATP hydrolysis to alter nucleosome positioning, and multiple independent clinical reports describe de novo or intragenic loss-of-function variants in CHD8 in individuals with ASD. Experimental suppression of CHD8 in ASD model systems recapitulates molecular phenotypes relevant to the disorder, and targeted SINEUP RNA–based restoration of CHD8 expression has been reported to rescue these CHD8-suppression–associated molecular abnormalities, underscoring both the centrality and partial reversibility of CHD8-dependent chromatin remodeling defects in ASD.

CHD2 is another chromodomain helicase DNA-binding ATPase in this intersection that contributes ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler activity. CHD2 has been implicated in epilepsy phenotypes, and studies of CHD2-associated epilepsy include CHD1, CHD4, CHD7 and CHD8 in broader discussions of chromatin remodeling proteins that influence neuronal excitability. The involvement of CHD2 in ATP-driven chromatin remodeling, together with its role in neurodevelopmental epilepsies that frequently overlap clinically and genetically with ASD, supports a pathogenic mechanism in which CHD2-mediated nucleosome remodeling influences neurodevelopmental trajectories relevant to ASD.

CHD1, CHD3, CHD4 and CHD7 complete the chromodomain helicase DNA-binding subgroup within this pathway. Each of these genes encodes an ATP-dependent helicase that modulates histone–DNA contacts, and functional work on CHD family remodelers in epilepsy and neurodevelopment highlights their shared capacity to remodel nucleosomes in neurons. In the context of ASD, the convergence of CHD1, CHD2, CHD4, CHD7 and CHD8 within this pathway points to a coordinated vulnerability of CHD-family ATPases whose disruption can alter chromatin accessibility at neurodevelopmental gene loci and thereby perturb neuronal circuit formation.

SMARCA1, SMARCA2 and SMARCA4 form a second functional cluster within the enriched intersection, comprising the ATPase subunits of SWI/SNF-class chromatin remodeling complexes. These ATP-dependent remodelers use the energy of ATP hydrolysis to slide or evict nucleosomes, complementing the remodeling activities of the CHD family and providing a parallel mechanism for dynamic regulation of chromatin structure in developing brain. The co-enrichment of CHD-family ATPases and SMARCA-family ATPases in this molecular function term indicates that both chromodomain-containing and SWI/SNF-type ATPases contribute to the ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling axis implicated in ASD.

The ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler activity pathway therefore highlights a core biochemical mechanism in ASD in which ATP-driven modulation of histone–DNA contacts is repeatedly targeted by genetic variation. The principal driver genes are CHD8 and CHD2, supported by additional CHD-family members (CHD1, CHD3, CHD4, CHD7) and the SWI/SNF ATPases SMARCA1, SMARCA2 and SMARCA4. Documented functional rescue of CHD8 suppression phenotypes, together with the recognized role of CHD2 and related remodelers in neurodevelopmental epilepsy, indicates that disruption of ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling constitutes a central axis of ASD risk within this gene set.

pathways.name: chromatin DNA binding
pathways.pathway_description: Binding to DNA that is assembled into chromatin. [GOC:mah]
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: This pathway reflects proteins that bind DNA within chromatin, a broad category encompassing many chromatin regulators and transcriptional co-factors, so it highlights general epigenetic and transcriptional control rather than a specific ASD mechanism. In ASD, disruption of chromatin DNA binding factors can alter large gene expression programs during brain development, providing a plausible route to widespread neurodevelopmental dysregulation.
Intersection-gene interpretation: ATRX and CHD4 are chromatin-associated regulators whose binding to DNA in chromatin can influence neuronal gene expression, and ATRX mutations have been directly linked to ASD, indicating that altered chromatin engagement by ATRX can contribute to ASD phenotypes. CREBBP is a histone acetyltransferase and transcriptional co-activator that binds chromatin and, together with related co-activators such as EP300 implicated in ASD, suggests that impaired recruitment of acetyltransferase complexes to chromatin may disturb expression of neurodevelopmental genes in ASD.
PubMed literature synthesis: Case reports and mouse models demonstrate that ATRX deficiency leads to altered brain structure and ASD, directly tying a chromatin DNA-binding factor to ASD-related neuroanatomical and behavioral changes. Broader ASD genetic surveys identifying CREBBP and other chromatin regulators (e.g., KDM6B, SMARCA4, HNRNPU) underscore that mutations in chromatin-binding and remodeling machinery are a recurrent theme in ASD, consistent with a shared mechanism of dysregulated chromatin-mediated transcription.
Cell/tissue context: The attached evidence supports effects in the brain, including altered brain structure in ATRX-deficient mouse models, but does not further resolve specific neuronal subtypes or brain regions beyond this general neural context.

paragraphs: 18 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in chromatin DNA binding (GO:0031490).

Among the genes with the clearest links to ASD in this pathway, ATRX encodes a chromatin-associated ATP-dependent remodeler that binds DNA within nucleosomal contexts and regulates large-scale chromatin architecture. An ATRX-deficient mouse model of autism spectrum disorder shows altered brain structure, indicating that disruption of ATRX-mediated chromatin–DNA interactions can perturb neuroanatomical development in vivo. Consistent with this experimental evidence, a clinical case report has described ASD caused by a mutation in ATRX, directly tying ATRX variants in humans to an ASD phenotype and supporting ATRX as a key chromatin DNA–binding driver in the disorder.

CREBBP and EP300 encode closely related histone acetyltransferors and transcriptional co-activators that bind promoter and enhancer DNA within chromatin through multiprotein complexes. Population-based sequencing in Middle Eastern cohorts has implicated CREBBP and KDM6B in the genetic landscape of ASD, highlighting that disruption of CREBBP-dependent chromatin binding and co-activator function contributes to disease risk.

HNRNPU and SMARCA4 further emphasize the convergence of ASD risk on chromatin DNA–bound regulators with mosaic or remodeling functions. Rates and distribution analyses of postzygotic mosaic mutations in ASD have identified HNRNPU and SMARCA4, suggesting that somatic disruption of their chromatin-associated activities in neural progenitors or developing neurons can contribute to ASD pathogenesis. HNRNPU encodes a nuclear RNA-binding protein that associates with chromatin and influences higher-order genome organization, whereas SMARCA4 encodes the ATPase subunit of a SWI/SNF-family chromatin remodeler that engages directly with nucleosomal DNA to reposition or evict nucleosomes.

The remaining genes can be grouped into three functional clusters based on their chromatin DNA–binding roles. A first cluster of chromatin remodelers and architectural factors—CHD4, CTCF, SMARCC2, and AHDC1—comprises genes that shape three-dimensional genome topology and nucleosome organization while bound to DNA within chromatin. A second cluster of histone- and nucleosome-associated genes—H1-4, H3-3B, and ACTB—includes core and linker histone components and an actin gene that participate in nucleoprotein filament or nucleosome structure while contacting chromatin DNA. A third cluster of transcriptional and epigenetic regulators with sequence- or context-specific chromatin binding—PAX6, TBR1, ZFX, KDM3B, and KDM6B—encompasses transcription factors and histone demethylases whose DNA occupancy in chromatin directly couples cis-regulatory recognition to the modification state of histone tails and transcriptional output in neural lineages.

Chromatin DNA binding enriches for ASD genes that directly engage nucleosomal DNA to coordinate transcriptional regulation, higher-order genome organization, and epigenetic state during brain development. The principal driver genes are ATRX, CREBBP, EP300, HNRNPU, SMARCA4, and KDM6B, which together are supported by genetic or functional evidence in ASD and exemplify distinct but convergent modes of chromatin engagement.

paragraphs: 54 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in RNA polymerase II cis-regulatory region sequence-specific DNA binding (GO:0000978).

Several genes in this pathway encode transcriptional regulators with direct evidence in autism spectrum disorder cohorts. CHD7 encodes a chromodomain helicase that binds cis-regulatory regions to modulate chromatin accessibility, and whole-genome sequencing of Japanese autism spectrum disorder trios has identified CHD7 variants in affected individuals, supporting a contributory role of CHD7-mediated enhancer regulation in at least a subset of cases. CHD2, another chromatin-remodeling gene with sequence-specific influence on regulatory DNA, has been implicated through disease similarity network analysis linking autism spectrum disorder with comorbid brain disorders, indicating that disruption of CHD2-controlled cis-regulatory programs may represent a shared molecular axis across neurodevelopmental phenotypes. KDM6B encodes a histone demethylase that recognizes promoter and enhancer regions of RNA polymerase II–transcribed genes, and genetic analyses in Middle Eastern populations with autism spectrum disorder have reported KDM6B variation, consistent with a model in which altered KDM6B-mediated interpretation of cis-regulatory elements contributes to regional or population-specific genetic risk.

Additional enriched genes reinforce a convergent role for cis-regulatory transcription factor function in autism spectrum disorder. HNRNPU, identified in studies of postzygotic mosaic mutations in autism spectrum disorder, participates in the recognition and processing of RNA derived from RNA polymerase II–driven loci and also associates with regulatory chromatin near promoters, indicating that mosaic perturbation of HNRNPU at cis-regulated genes can influence neural gene expression in a cell-lineage–restricted manner. BCL11A, reported in exploratory autoantibody profiling in autism spectrum disorder, encodes a sequence-specific transcription factor that binds promoter and enhancer regions of RNA polymerase II target genes, raising the possibility that both genetic and immune-mediated interference with BCL11A-bound cis-regulatory sites modulates neurodevelopmental transcriptional programs. The transcription factor CHD7, together with CHD2 and KDM6B, therefore represents a core group of cis-regulatory effectors with documented involvement in autism spectrum disorder genetic studies, anchoring the functional interpretation of this pathway.

Beyond these directly documented genes, most of the remaining intersection genes encode transcription factors or chromatin-linked DNA-binding proteins that recognize specific cis-regulatory motifs upstream of RNA polymerase II transcription start sites. A large cluster comprises cortical and neuronal lineage transcription factors with sequence-specific promoter or enhancer binding, including ARX, CUX2, EBF3, FOXP2, IRX5, MEF2C, MEIS2, MKX, MSX2, NFIB, NFIX, NR2F1, PAX5, PAX6, POU3F3, RFX3, RFX4, RFX7, RORA, RORB, SATB1, SATB2, SOX5, SOX6, TBR1, TBX1, TCF4, TCF7L2, TFE3, ZBTB20, ZBTB7A, ZFHX3, ZFHX4, ZFX, ZNF865 and NACC1, which collectively define neuronal subtype identity and connectivity through cis-regulatory sequence recognition. A second functional cluster consists of chromatin- and epigenetic-modifying factors that localize to regulatory regions of RNA polymerase II genes, such as CHD7, CHD2, DNMT3A, HDAC4, H3-3B, HIVEP2, HNRNPU, KDM2B, KDM6B, NSD1, SATB1, SATB2, TET3, YY1, CTCF and DHX9, integrating DNA sequence recognition with histone modification and higher-order chromatin architecture at promoters and enhancers. A third cluster is formed by nuclear receptor and signal-responsive transcription factors that bind specific hormone- or activity-regulated motifs near RNA polymerase II start sites, including NR3C2, NR4A2, RORA, RORB, TCF4, TCF7L2 and RFX family genes, which are positioned to couple extracellular signals to changes in cis-regulatory transcription in developing neural circuits.

Enrichment of these 54 genes in RNA polymerase II cis-regulatory region sequence-specific DNA binding indicates that disruption of transcription factor recognition of promoter and enhancer sequences is a central axis of genetic risk for autism spectrum disorder. The principal driver genes are CHD7, CHD2 and KDM6B, which are supported by direct autism spectrum disorder genetic studies and occupy key positions at the interface of cis-regulatory DNA binding and chromatin remodeling. HNRNPU and BCL11A provide additional mechanistic support by linking postzygotic mosaicism and immune reactivity, respectively, to factors that act at RNA polymerase II–regulated loci. Documented physical and functional interactions among chromatin remodelers and transcription factors, including those between CHD7, CHD2, KDM6B and other regulatory proteins such as CTCF and YY1, further emphasize that autism spectrum disorder risk in this pathway likely arises from perturbation of multi-protein complexes that coordinate sequence-specific recognition of cis-regulatory DNA with appropriate transcriptional output in the developing brain.

pathways.pathway_description: The part of a synapse that is part of the post-synaptic cell. [GOC:dos]
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: Postsynaptic structures integrate synaptic inputs and support plasticity, and their disruption is a central hypothesis for ASD, where altered excitatory–inhibitory balance and synaptic signaling are frequently observed. Enrichment of postsynaptic components in ASD-related protein interaction networks suggests that postsynaptic dysfunction contributes to cognitive and social phenotypes.
Intersection-gene interpretation: The intersection genes ACTB, AGO2, ANK2, ANK3, and ANKS1B encode cytoskeletal scaffolds and RNA-silencing machinery that help organize and regulate postsynaptic signaling complexes. ANK2, directly implicated in ASD by structural variants, points to disturbed anchoring of ion channels and receptors at the postsynaptic membrane as a specific mechanism for synaptic dysfunction.
PubMed literature synthesis: ASD genetics studies highlighting ANK2, FMR1, GRIN2B, CACNA1C, CUL3, and DMD converge on postsynaptic signaling, receptor function, and spine structure as recurrently affected processes. Additional work on chromosome 21 protein–protein interactions and RBFOX1 regulation supports a broader model in which postsynaptic protein networks and activity-dependent RNA regulation are enriched for ASD-associated perturbations.
Cell/tissue context: The evidence points to postsynaptic compartments of neurons in the central nervous system, particularly cortical and other brain synapses involved in cognition and speech. No non-neuronal cell types are directly supported by the supplied pathway-level evidence. [PMID:35914814] [PMID:42079041]

pathways.name: dendrite
pathways.pathway_description: A neuron projection that has a short, tapering, morphology. Dendrites receive and integrate signals from other neurons or from sensory stimuli, and conduct nerve impulses towards the axon or the cell body. In most neurons, the impulse is conveyed from dendrites to axon via the cell body, but in some types of unipolar neuron, the impulse does not travel via the cell body. [GOC:aruk, GOC:bc, GOC:dos, GOC:mah, GOC:nln, ISBN:0198506732]
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: The dendrite pathway highlights that abnormalities in dendritic growth, branching, and synaptic integration are likely contributors to ASD, consistent with neuropathological observations of altered neuronal connectivity. Disrupted dendritic architecture can impair how neurons receive and integrate synaptic inputs, leading to circuit-level dysfunction characteristic of ASD.
Intersection-gene interpretation: ADNP and ANKS1B are regulators of neuronal development and synaptic organization whose dysfunction could impair dendritic maturation and spine formation, while ANK3 anchors ion channels at neuronal membranes and may influence dendritic excitability. CACNA1C-mediated calcium influx and AGO2-dependent post-transcriptional regulation can both shape dendritic development and plasticity, suggesting that multiple molecular layers converge on dendritic structure and function in ASD.
PubMed literature synthesis: Pathway-level studies showing that ASD susceptibility genes such as TAOK2 affect basal dendrite formation, and that TRPC4 stabilizes dendrite branches, support a model in which genetic risk converges on dendritic morphogenesis and maintenance. Gene-level ASD associations for CACNA1C, CNTNAP2, FMR1, DSCAM, DYRK1A, and GRIN2B—many of which are known regulators of dendritic growth and synaptic structure—reinforce dendritic development and stability as a key mechanistic axis in ASD.
Cell/tissue context: The evidence points to dendritic abnormalities in neocortical neurons, particularly in regions such as the neocortex where TAOK2-dependent basal dendrite formation has been implicated, and more broadly in limbic circuits where TRPC4-regulated dendritic stabilization influences behavior. paragraphs: 52 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in dendrite (GO:0030425).

Several of the enriched genes encode postsynaptic scaffold or receptor components that occupy dendritic domains critical for excitatory synaptic signaling. SHANK2 encodes a core postsynaptic density scaffold at dendritic spines, and mutations in SHANK2 that are associated with autism spectrum disorder have been shown to induce hyperconnectivity of human neurons, implicating dendritic spine organization in disease-related network dysfunction. DLG4 encodes a major postsynaptic density scaffold that organizes glutamate receptors and associated signaling complexes in dendrites and directly participates in the PSD-95–neuroligin complex that has been mechanistically linked to autism spectrum disorder, so its dendritic localization is likely to be central to perturbed synaptic integration. The glutamate receptor genes GRIN2B and GRIN2A encode subunits of the NMDA receptor that are highly enriched in dendritic spines; de novo GRIN2B mutations have been repeatedly identified in autism spectrum disorder cohorts, including studies that specifically highlight GRIN2B among the most penetrant de novo variants, reinforcing the relevance of dendritic NMDA receptor composition to the disorder.

A second group of notable genes encodes ion channels and signaling kinases that shape dendritic excitability and plasticity. CACNA1C encodes the pore-forming subunit of an L-type voltage-gated calcium channel that is prominently localized to dendrites where it couples depolarization to calcium influx; genetic studies in diverse populations, including Pakistani and East African autism spectrum disorder cohorts, have identified CACNA1C variants among the recurrent risk alleles, supporting a contribution of altered dendritic calcium signaling to autism spectrum disorder etiology. CNTNAP2 encodes a neurexin family cell-adhesion molecule that concentrates at specific neuronal compartments, including dendritic regions, and is repeatedly implicated in autism spectrum disorder by both familial and case–control sequencing studies, including work that links CNTNAP2 variation to the broader neuropathology of the disorder. FMR1 encodes an RNA-binding protein that is highly enriched in dendritic shafts and spines, where it regulates local translation; loss of FMR1 causes a syndromic form of autism spectrum disorder, and neuropathological and animal model work consistently highlights abnormal dendritic spine structure and density as a hallmark of FMR1-related pathology, underscoring the direct involvement of dendritic compartments in disease expression.

Additional enriched genes form coherent functional clusters within dendrites. A glutamatergic receptor and synaptic signaling cluster includes GRIN1, GRIA2, GRIA3, NLGN2, NLGN4X, SYNGAP1, FRMPD4, TANC2, CAMK2A, PPP3CA, PAK1, MAPK8IP3, and RELN, all of which encode dendritically localized receptors, adhesion molecules, or signal transducers that participate in postsynaptic integration and plasticity at excitatory synapses. An inhibitory synaptic and GABAergic signaling cluster, comprising GABRA3, GABRB2, and GABRB3, encodes GABAA receptor subunits that reside at dendritic inhibitory synapses and contribute to the balance of excitation and inhibition in dendritic arbors. A dendritic transport and cytoskeletal organization cluster includes KIF1A, KIF5C, MAP1A, ANK3, ANKS1B, DSCAM, and SHANK2, which encode structural or transport components required for the positioning of receptors and scaffolds within dendrites. A signaling and growth-regulation cluster contains MTOR, PTEN, NF1, NTRK2, CDKL5, DYRK1A, FGF13, PTCHD1, AGO2, GIGYF2, KLHL20, ZMYND8, SNX14, CAPRIN1, HNRNPU, SLC9A6, PPP1R9B, and SYN1, encoding proteins that reside in dendrites to regulate protein synthesis, signal transduction, membrane trafficking, or ion homeostasis. Co-localization of these gene products within dendrites indicates that many autism spectrum disorder risk genes operate in shared subcellular territories, but enrichment in this cellular compartment alone does not establish a single common molecular mechanism across them.

The dendrite enrichment term indicates that a substantial fraction of autism spectrum disorder risk genes encode products that co-localize to dendritic shafts and spines, a cellular compartment that is itself a prominent site of neuropathology and synaptic dysfunction in the disorder. The principal driver genes are SHANK2, GRIN2B, and CACNA1C, which combine strong genetic evidence for autism spectrum disorder with central roles in dendritic postsynaptic organization and excitability. Documented interactions within this set, such as the participation of DLG4 in the PSD-95–neuroligin complex that also includes neuroligins encoded by NLGN2 and NLGN4X, exemplify how multiple enriched genes converge at dendritic synaptic junctions. This pathway therefore emphasizes dendritic compartments as a major anatomical locus at which diverse autism spectrum disorder risk genes exert their effects, without implying that all such genes act through a single shared pathway.

pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: This pathway represents axonal structure and function, including growth, guidance, and impulse conduction, processes that are frequently altered in ASD through atypical connectivity, pruning, and myelination. Disruption of axon development or maintenance can lead to miswired neural circuits and abnormal signal timing, providing a mechanistic basis for ASD-related network dysfunction.
Intersection-gene interpretation: ACTB encodes β-actin, a core cytoskeletal component required for axon extension and structural dynamics, so its involvement suggests that cytoskeletal regulation of axon morphology may be relevant to ASD. ADGRL1, ADNP, ANK3, and ATP1A1 contribute to axon adhesion, transcriptional regulation of neuronal development, axon initial segment organization, and ionic gradients for action potential propagation, respectively, indicating that multiple aspects of axonal integrity and excitability are represented in this ASD-enriched pathway.
PubMed literature synthesis: Studies showing that CHD8 deficiency impairs axon development and migration of cortical neurons, and that age-related differences in axon pruning and myelination may alter neural signaling in ASD, directly link axonal development and remodeling to ASD pathophysiology. Additional ASD literature on genes such as CNTNAP2, DSCAM, FMR1, NF1, and CDKL5, which influence axon guidance, synaptic connectivity, or myelination, reinforces that axonal and connectivity defects are a recurrent mechanistic theme in ASD.

pathways.name: glutamatergic synapse
pathways.pathway_description: A synapse that uses glutamate as a neurotransmitter. [GOC:dos]
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: Glutamatergic synapses are central to excitatory neurotransmission, and convergent ASD work implicates altered glutamate signaling and synaptic organization in disrupted excitation–inhibition balance and circuit plasticity. The attached pathway-level literature directly links glutamatergic synapse dysfunction to ASD-like behaviors and neuronal hyperexcitability, supporting this as a core mechanistic axis in the disorder.
Intersection-gene interpretation: Within this pathway, CDKL5 is a synapse-associated kinase whose disruption can impair glutamatergic synaptic development or signaling, providing a plausible route to ASD-related circuit dysfunction. Other intersecting genes such as ACTB, AGO2, ATP2B1, and BRAF participate in cytoskeletal structure, RNA regulation, calcium extrusion, and intracellular signaling at glutamatergic synapses, suggesting that diverse molecular perturbations at these synapses can converge on similar ASD-relevant phenotypes.
PubMed literature synthesis: Pathway-level studies on glutamatergic synapses in ASD, NRXN1+/− iPSC-derived neurons, and Tshz3 deletion models collectively support that altered glutamate synapse formation and function produce ASD-like behaviors and increased neuronal excitability. Gene-level evidence for CDKL5 mutations in ASD further ties synaptic kinase dysfunction to this glutamatergic framework, while additional ASD genes (CNTNAP2, NLGN3, NRXN1, SHANK3, NF1, HRAS) reinforce that multiple synaptic organizers and signaling molecules converge on glutamatergic circuit pathology.
Cell/tissue context: The evidence supports involvement of cortical and corticostriatal glutamatergic neurons and their synapses, with additional relevance to general excitatory neuronal populations where glutamate is the primary neurotransmitter. [PMID:36434055] [PMID:34525970] [PMID:31060802]

paragraphs: 37 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in glutamatergic synapse (GO:0098978).

Among the genes previously implicated most directly in ASD are NRXN1 and SHANK3, both of which encode core organizers of excitatory synapses. NRXN1 encodes a presynaptic cell-adhesion molecule that localizes to glutamatergic terminals and interacts trans-synaptically with postsynaptic partners; ASD-associated NRXN1 deletions and loss-of-function mutations have been repeatedly reported, and neurophysiological work on NRXN1alpha(+/−) neurons demonstrates increased excitability in induced pluripotent stem cell–derived neuronal models of ASD. SHANK3 encodes a prominent postsynaptic density scaffold at glutamatergic synapses, and SHANK3 mutations and copy-number alterations define one of the most robust single-gene links to ASD, with patients often presenting with ASD alongside intellectual disability and language impairment, underscoring the relevance of postsynaptic structural disruption at glutamatergic synapses in this disorder.

Several additional postsynaptic and signaling genes enriched in this term have been tied experimentally or clinically to ASD-related phenotypes. TRIO encodes a Rho-GEF that localizes to excitatory synapses; ASD/ID-associated TRIO mutations have been shown to disrupt neuroligin 1–mediated synaptogenesis, directly linking altered synaptic structural signaling to ASD. SYNGAP1 encodes a Ras/Rap GTPase-activating protein concentrated at glutamatergic postsynaptic densities, and developmental Syngap1 haploinsufficiency in medial ganglionic eminence–derived interneurons impairs auditory cortex activity, social behavior, and fear-extinction in model systems, providing a mechanistic bridge between glutamatergic circuit dysfunction and core ASD-like behaviors. NF1, which encodes a Ras-GAP that can localize to synaptic compartments, has been associated with ASD in children with neurofibromatosis type 1, where a substantial subset of affected individuals meet diagnostic criteria for ASD or display significant autistic traits, consistent with glutamatergic synapse–localized Ras signaling perturbation contributing to ASD in this genetic context.

A broader group of enriched genes encodes cell-adhesion and trans-synaptic organizing molecules essential for glutamatergic synapse architecture. CNTNAP2, NLGN3, NLGN4X, NRXN2, NRXN3, LRRC4C, SLITRK2, NTNG1, and NTNG2 all encode membrane proteins that reside at or bridge pre- and postsynaptic membranes at glutamatergic contacts, where disease-linked members such as CNTNAP2, NLGN3, and NRXN1 have been specifically highlighted in ASD-focused clinical and neuropathological studies. Another cluster comprises postsynaptic density scaffolds and adaptors—DLG4, SHANK3, PPFIA3, PPP1R9B, SYNGAP1, and SPTBN1—that assemble multiprotein signaling platforms beneath glutamatergic receptors. A signaling-regulatory cluster, including BRAF, HRAS, NF1, PPP3CA, CNKSR2, TRIO, and CUL3, contributes Ras/MAPK and phosphatase-dependent modulation within the glutamatergic synapse compartment. Finally, presynaptic release and vesicle–fusion machinery, represented by STXBP1, SYT1, NBEA, and SLC9A6, along with more ubiquitous structural and regulatory components such as ACTB, CHD4, CORO1A, CTNNB1, GRIN2A, HNRNPD, AGO2, UBE3A, ATP2B1, and STXBP1, populate the molecular environment of the glutamatergic synapse without necessarily sharing a single mechanistic role; their co-localization within this compartment highlights a convergence of ASD genes at excitatory synaptic sites but does not by itself establish a common pathogenic mechanism.

The glutamatergic synapse pathway therefore contributes a spatially coherent view of ASD risk genes converging on the cellular compartment where excitatory transmission is executed and regulated. The principal driver genes in this enrichment are NRXN1, SHANK3, and SYNGAP1, which together anchor pre- and postsynaptic specializations and link structural synapse organization to Ras-dependent signaling and circuit-level phenotypes relevant to ASD. Well-documented interactions between the encoded proteins, such as the trans-synaptic binding of NRXN1 to neuroligins and the incorporation of SHANK3 and SYNGAP1 into the DLG4-centered postsynaptic density complex, support the interpretation that perturbations in a physically interacting glutamatergic synaptic network can underlie a subset of ASD presentations. This enrichment emphasizes that disruption of excitatory synapse architecture and signaling is a central axis of ASD neurobiology supported by convergent genetic evidence.

pathways.pathway_description: Long-term potentiation
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: Long-term potentiation (LTP) is a core cellular mechanism of learning and memory, and its impairment is a plausible contributor to ASD-related deficits in symbolic learning, cognition, and sensory processing. Altered LTP can disrupt the refinement of neural circuits, leading to atypical information processing and behavioral phenotypes.
Intersection-gene interpretation: The intersection genes BRAF, CACNA1C, CAMK2A, CAMK2B, and CAMK2D encode key kinases and calcium channels that transduce synaptic activity into long-lasting changes in synaptic strength. CACNA1C, directly associated with ASD, links voltage-gated calcium influx to downstream CAMK2-dependent signaling cascades that are essential for LTP induction and maintenance.
PubMed literature synthesis: ASD genetic studies implicating GRIN2B, CREBBP, GRIA2, and EP300, together with work on DYRK1A signaling and SCN2A-associated cerebellar plasticity, converge on synaptic plasticity pathways as recurrently disrupted in ASD. A family study of symbolic learning and synaptic plasticity in ASD further supports the idea that LTP-related mechanisms are functionally altered in affected individuals.
Cell/tissue context: The evidence supports LTP mechanisms in neurons of the brain, including hippocampal and cerebellar circuits involved in learning, memory, and sensory reflex modulation. Specific non-neuronal tissues are not indicated by the supplied evidence. [PMID:42405393] [PMID:38412857] [PMID:36504626]

paragraphs: 14 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in Long-term potentiation (KEGG:04720).

Among the postsynaptic glutamate receptor genes, GRIN2B and GRIN2A encode NMDA receptor subunits that are central to calcium-dependent induction of long-term potentiation, and GRIN1 encodes the obligatory NMDA receptor subunit GluN1, whose alternative splicing has been directly implicated in the control of long-term synaptic potentiation and learning. Rare potentially damaging variants in GRIN2B have been repeatedly identified in individuals with ASD and related neurodevelopmental conditions, and GRIN2B has also been linked to ASD in broader genetic surveys and neuropathological syntheses, supporting a robust association between NMDA receptor dysfunction and ASD phenotypes. GRIA2, encoding an AMPA receptor subunit, contributes to fast excitatory transmission and synaptic strengthening, and rare variants in GRIA2 have been reported in ASD cohorts, further implicating glutamatergic synaptic transmission in the disorder.

Two transcriptional coactivator genes, CREBBP and EP300, occupy a downstream position in the Long-term potentiation pathway where calcium- and kinase-dependent signaling converges on the nucleus to remodel gene expression. The pathway-level literature on synaptic plasticity in ASD, including studies of atypical plasticity probed with rTMS and of symbolic learning deficits, aligns with the positioning of CREBBP and EP300 as nuclear effectors of activity-dependent transcriptional programs triggered by Long-term potentiation.

Within the Long-term potentiation pathway map, BRAF, HRAS and RPS6KA3 form a contiguous signaling gene list linking membrane receptor activation to nuclear responses. HRAS acts in the proximal Ras node, BRAF serves as a canonical Raf-family kinase immediately downstream, and RPS6KA3 functions as a MAPK-activated kinase that phosphorylates nuclear substrates including transcription factors involved in plasticity-related gene expression.

The remaining enriched genes cluster into three functional segments along the KEGG Long-term potentiation map. First, CACNA1C lies at the membrane-proximal calcium entry step as an L-type voltage-gated calcium channel subunit, coupling depolarization to the intracellular calcium transients that initiate Long-term potentiation and providing a direct link to calcium-dependent cascades also represented in other KEGG signaling maps. Second, CAMK2A, CAMK2B and CAMK2D, together with PPP3CA, constitute a calcium-sensitive kinase–phosphatase gene list: CAMK2 family genes encode Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent kinases that phosphorylate postsynaptic receptors and scaffolds to stabilize potentiated synapses, while PPP3CA encodes the catalytic subunit of calcineurin, a Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase that provides feedback regulation of these phosphorylation events; this gene list interfaces with adjacent KEGG pathways for calcium signaling and MAPK signaling via shared reliance on calmodulin and downstream transcription factors. Third, the nuclear coactivators CREBBP and EP300 form a chromatin-modifying cluster that translates synaptic activity into long-term transcriptional changes, thereby serving as an output node of Long-term potentiation that can influence neuronal connectivity and learning-related gene expression.

The enriched Long-term potentiation pathway highlights a mechanistic axis from NMDA and AMPA receptor activation through Ras–MAPK signaling to chromatin remodeling, and connects synaptic plasticity abnormalities described in ASD rTMS and learning studies with specific ASD-linked genes. The principal driver genes are GRIN2B, CREBBP and EP300, which are supported by direct genetic or experimental evidence in ASD and occupy key convergence points for calcium influx and nuclear transcriptional control. Within this framework, GRIN1, GRIN2A and GRIA2 interact functionally with GRIN2B at the postsynaptic density to initiate Long-term potentiation, while BRAF, HRAS and RPS6KA3 constitute an intervening kinase cascade that relays these signals to CREBBP and EP300 in the nucleus. This configuration supports a model in which ASD risk variants perturb the induction and stabilization phases of Long-term potentiation through coordinated disruption of glutamatergic signaling, kinase pathways and epigenetic regulation of activity-dependent genes.

pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: The glutamatergic synapse pathway implicates altered excitatory neurotransmission and synaptic plasticity as core mechanisms in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), consistent with models of disrupted excitation–inhibition balance and corticostriatal circuit dysfunction. Pathway-level evidence links glutamatergic synaptic abnormalities to ASD-like behaviors and increased neuronal excitability in patient-derived neurons.
Intersection-gene interpretation: CACNA1A and CACNA1C encode voltage-gated calcium channel subunits that couple presynaptic depolarization to glutamate release and postsynaptic signaling, so their disruption could alter synaptic strength and plasticity at glutamatergic synapses. DLG4 (PSD-95) organizes postsynaptic receptor and scaffold complexes, while GNAI1 and GNB2 mediate G-protein signaling that modulates glutamate receptor function, together suggesting that both structural and signaling components of the glutamatergic synapse are vulnerable points for ASD-related dysfunction.
PubMed literature synthesis: Pathway-level studies describing “glutamatergic synapse in autism” and ASD-like phenotypes in NRXN1α(+/−) iPSC-derived neurons and Tshz3 deletion models converge on the idea that perturbations of glutamatergic synaptic organization and transmission are sufficient to drive ASD-relevant behavioral and electrophysiological phenotypes. Gene-level ASD studies of GRIN2B and SHANK family proteins, which are core postsynaptic glutamatergic components, further support a mechanistic model in which disruption of glutamate receptor complexes and their scaffolds at excitatory synapses contributes to ASD.
Cell/tissue context: The evidence supports involvement of cortical and corticostriatal glutamatergic synapses, particularly in prefrontal and striatal circuits where Tshz3-dependent and NRXN1α-dependent alterations have been linked to ASD-like behaviors. [PMID:36434055] [PMID:34525970] [PMID:31060802]
