paragraphs: 13 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in Glutamatergic synapse (KEGG:04724).

SHANK3 and SHANK2 encode core postsynaptic scaffold proteins that organize glutamate receptors and signaling complexes at excitatory synapses, and both have well-established links to ASD. Multiple independent studies identify SHANK3 as an ASD-associated gene, with disruptive mutations frequently observed in individuals with ASD and related neurodevelopmental phenotypes, and polymorphisms in SHANK3 have been associated with altered susceptibility to ASD in case–control cohorts. SHANK proteins more broadly, including SHANK2 and SHANK3, are consistently implicated in ASD, where deleterious variation typically presents with social-communication deficits and restricted behaviors, indicating that perturbation of SHANK-dependent synaptic architecture is a recurrent mechanism in ASD neuropathology.

GRIN2B and GRIN2A, together with GRIN1, encode subunits of NMDA-type ionotropic glutamate receptors that mediate Ca2+-permeable synaptic transmission and are central to synaptic plasticity in the glutamatergic synapse map. GRIN2B has been repeatedly highlighted in ASD genetic studies, including in cohorts from Vietnamese children with ASD, and is also discussed in broader neuropathological surveys of ASD and animal models, where GRIN2B disruption is linked to abnormal cortical circuitry and cognitive impairments. In these contexts, GRIN2B variation is associated with ASD and intellectual disability, supporting a role for altered NMDA receptor composition and signaling in the ASD phenotype.

The remaining genes enriched in the glutamatergic synapse pathway cluster into functionally coherent gene lists spanning ligand-gated receptors, voltage-gated Ca2+ entry, G-protein signaling, and Ca2+-dependent effectors within the KEGG map. GRIA2 and GRIA3 encode AMPA-type glutamate receptor subunits that operate immediately downstream of presynaptic glutamate release to mediate fast excitatory transmission; their activity is scaffolded and modulated by DLG4, a postsynaptic density protein that links ionotropic receptors to SHANK-based complexes at the synapse. CACNA1A and CACNA1C encode pore-forming α1 subunits of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels that reside upstream of Ca2+-dependent signaling, coupling membrane depolarization to intracellular Ca2+ influx and thereby shaping both neurotransmitter release and postsynaptic plasticity. GNAI1 and GNB2 encode G-protein subunits that participate in metabotropic signaling branches of the glutamatergic synapse map, modulating downstream second-messenger cascades that converge on synaptic efficacy. PPP3CA encodes the catalytic subunit of calcineurin, a Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase positioned downstream of NMDA receptor– and voltage-gated channel–mediated Ca2+ entry, which regulates dephosphorylation events affecting receptor trafficking and synaptic remodeling. Within the KEGG glutamatergic synapse diagram, these genes are concentrated in the postsynaptic compartment and the immediate upstream Ca2+ influx and G-protein signaling nodes, forming a largely contiguous block from receptor activation (GRIA2, GRIA3, GRIN1, GRIN2A, GRIN2B) through membrane excitability (CACNA1A, CACNA1C) to intracellular Ca2+-dependent effectors (PPP3CA), with cross-talk to adjacent calcium signaling and long-term potentiation maps mediated by shared use of NMDA receptors, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and calcineurin. The postsynaptic scaffolding components SHANK2, SHANK3, and DLG4 physically and functionally interconnect these elements, reinforcing a coherent synaptic signaling gene list rather than scattered, isolated hits.

The glutamatergic synapse pathway contributes a mechanistically unified axis of ASD risk centered on postsynaptic receptor composition, scaffolding, and Ca2+-dependent signaling at excitatory synapses. The principal driver genes are SHANK3, SHANK2, and GRIN2B, which have direct and recurrent genetic links to ASD and anchor key nodes in the postsynaptic density and NMDA receptor complex. Documented interactions among the intersection genes, particularly the established functional and structural cooperation between SHANK proteins, DLG4, and NMDA/AMPA receptor subunits, highlight a convergent disruption of excitatory synaptic organization in ASD. This enriched pathway thereby situates multiple ASD genes within a shared circuit-level mechanism of altered glutamatergic transmission and plasticity.

pathways.name: Dopaminergic synapse
pathways.pathway_description: Dopaminergic synapse
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: This pathway captures calcium-dependent signaling and kinase cascades at dopaminergic synapses that tune neurotransmitter release and postsynaptic responsiveness, processes frequently implicated in ASD-related alterations of reward processing, motivation, and motor function. Disruption of dopaminergic synaptic signaling can plausibly converge with glutamatergic receptor abnormalities (e.g., GRIN2A/GRIN2B) and epilepsy-associated channelopathies to produce the excitation–inhibition and plasticity imbalances observed in ASD.
Intersection-gene interpretation: CACNA1A and CACNA1C encode voltage-gated calcium channel subunits that control presynaptic calcium influx and dopamine release, and CACNA1A variants have been directly associated with co-occurring epilepsy and ASD, supporting a role for aberrant calcium entry at dopaminergic terminals in ASD. CAMK2A, CAMK2B, and CAMK2D encode Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent kinases that translate dopaminergic activity into changes in synaptic strength; their dysfunction would be expected to impair activity-dependent plasticity at dopaminergic synapses relevant to ASD phenotypes.
PubMed literature synthesis: ASD genetic studies implicating GRIN2A, GRIN2B, SCN1A, and CACNA1A, together with neuropathology and animal model work, support a broader theme of ion channel and glutamatergic receptor dysfunction converging on synaptic signaling pathways that include dopaminergic circuits. Additional ASD-focused studies on long non-coding RNAs, CMV-induced dysregulation of neurodevelopmental pathways in cerebral organoids, and germline functional variants further reinforce that dopaminergic synapse components lie within a wider network of neurodevelopmental and synaptic genes perturbed in ASD.
Cell/tissue context: The evidence supports involvement of dopaminergic synapses in brain regions where these channels and kinases operate, such as midbrain dopaminergic neurons and their cortical and striatal targets, but specific anatomical loci are not resolved beyond dopaminergic synapses by the supplied evidence. [PMID:33193567] [PMID:38504123] [PMID:41763521]

paragraphs: 17 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in Dopaminergic synapse (KEGG:04728).

Among the intersection genes, GRIN2A and GRIN2B encode NMDA-type glutamate receptor subunits that occupy a central position in postsynaptic signal integration within dopaminergic synapses, where NMDA receptor activity modulates dopamine-dependent plasticity. Multiple sequencing studies in ASD cohorts have identified rare, likely disruptive variants in GRIN2A and GRIN2B, and mutation screening of GRIN2B in a Japanese population has specifically implicated this gene in both schizophrenia and ASD, supporting a role for perturbed NMDA receptor-mediated signaling in neurodevelopmental phenotypes. SCN1A, which encodes a voltage-gated sodium channel alpha subunit critical for action potential initiation and propagation, is recurrently mutated in children with ASD and regression, and in cohorts with co-occurring epilepsy and ASD, underscoring that altered neuronal excitability at dopaminergic synapses contributes to a combined epilepsy–ASD phenotype. CACNA1A, encoding a high-voltage-activated P/Q-type calcium channel that couples membrane depolarization to calcium influx at presynaptic and postsynaptic sites, is likewise implicated in children with both ASD and epilepsy, further tying calcium-dependent synaptic transmission in dopaminergic circuits to ASD-related clinical presentations.

GRIA2 and GRIA3, which encode AMPA-type glutamate receptor subunits, and GRIN2A/GRIN2B together define a substantial postsynaptic glutamatergic receptor gene list embedded within the Dopaminergic synapse map, downstream of dopaminergic modulation and upstream of intracellular kinase cascades that drive synaptic plasticity. CAMK2A, CAMK2B, and CAMK2D encode subunits of calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II, a key postsynaptic effector activated by calcium influx through NMDA and voltage-gated calcium channels, which in turn regulates receptor trafficking and spine structure; their enrichment points to altered calcium-dependent decoding of dopaminergic and glutamatergic signals in ASD. KIF5C, a kinesin family motor protein, supports axonal and dendritic transport of synaptic components along microtubules in dopaminergic neurons, positioning it immediately downstream of activity-dependent signaling in the pathway map where it can influence the distribution of receptors and signaling complexes that shape synaptic efficacy.

PPP3CA, encoding the catalytic subunit of the calcium/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase calcineurin, and PPP2CA together with its regulatory subunits PPP2R5C and PPP2R5D, which form the phosphatase PP2A holoenzyme, cluster as major phosphatase components that counterbalance kinase activity in the Dopaminergic synapse pathway; they act downstream of calcium influx and G protein signaling to dephosphorylate receptors and ion channels, thereby modulating synaptic responsiveness and plasticity. GNAI1 and GNB2 form part of the heterotrimeric G protein complex that transduces signals from dopamine and other G protein-coupled receptors to intracellular effectors such as adenylyl cyclase and downstream kinases and phosphatases, situating them in the proximal signal transduction layer of the KEGG map. SCN1A, CACNA1A, CACNA1C, and the glutamate receptors occupy the voltage- and ligand-gated ion channel branch, which feeds into the CAMK2 and PPP3CA/PP2A phosphoregulation gene list; this branch in turn connects to adjacent KEGG synaptic maps, including glutamatergic synapse, through shared NMDA and AMPA receptor components and shared calcium-dependent signaling cascades.

The enrichment of these 17 genes in the Dopaminergic synapse pathway indicates that ASD risk converges on a contiguous postsynaptic signaling branch that links voltage-gated ion channels, glutamate receptors, calcium-dependent kinases, and phosphatases within dopaminergic circuits, rather than being scattered uniformly across presynaptic release machinery or distal transcriptional outputs. The principal driver genes are GRIN2A, GRIN2B, SCN1A, and CACNA1A, which are supported by direct ASD genetic evidence and occupy high-leverage positions in controlling synaptic excitability and plasticity. Documented clinical co-occurrence of epilepsy and ASD in carriers of SCN1A and CACNA1A variants aligns with their shared placement in the ion channel segment of the Dopaminergic synapse map, upstream of CAMK2 and PPP3CA/PP2A signaling. The strong representation of interacting proteins—such as SCN1A and CACNA1A converging on CAMK2 activation, with PPP3CA and PP2A components providing reciprocal dephosphorylation—supports a model in which dysregulated phosphorylation cycles at dopaminergic postsynapses are a key mechanistic axis of ASD risk in this pathway.

pathways.name: cAMP signaling pathway
pathways.pathway_description: cAMP signaling pathway
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: The cAMP signaling pathway is a key second-messenger system that modulates neuronal excitability, synaptic plasticity, and gene transcription, processes frequently altered in ASD. Dysregulated cAMP signaling can therefore provide a mechanistic link between upstream genetic or epigenetic insults and downstream changes in synaptic function and behavior.
Intersection-gene interpretation: BRAF and CACNA1C can influence cAMP-related signaling cascades and calcium-dependent modulation of cAMP effectors, while ATP1A1, ATP1A3, and ATP2B1 regulate ionic gradients and calcium homeostasis that shape cAMP-responsive signaling in neurons. Perturbations in these intersecting genes could alter how neurons integrate cAMP signals, leading to abnormal synaptic plasticity and network activity relevant to ASD.
PubMed literature synthesis: Pathway-level analyses of microRNA-targeted signaling and transcriptomic changes in ASD-like models highlight cAMP signaling as a recurrently perturbed pathway in ASD. Gene-level ASD studies implicating CREBBP, EP300, GRIN2B, and GRIA2 further support that cAMP-dependent transcriptional coactivators and glutamatergic signaling components are embedded in cAMP-regulated networks that are disrupted in ASD.
Cell/tissue context: The evidence supports involvement of neurons, particularly glutamatergic neurons where cAMP signaling modulates excitability and synaptic plasticity. [PMID:32895046] [PMID:42158647]

paragraphs: 20 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in cAMP signaling pathway (KEGG:04024).

Among the glutamatergic synaptic regulators enriched in this pathway, GRIN2B has the strongest documented link to autism spectrum disorder, with multiple studies identifying rare, potentially damaging variants in individuals with ASD and related neurodevelopmental phenotypes. GRIN2B encodes an NMDA receptor subunit that contributes to Ca2+-permeable glutamate receptors positioned downstream of cAMP-sensitive signaling gene lists; perturbation of this receptor’s function can alter activity-dependent signaling to nuclear effectors captured in this pathway. GRIA2, which encodes an AMPA receptor subunit, has likewise been implicated in the genetic landscape of autism spectrum disorder, supporting a convergence of ASD-related variation on ionotropic glutamate receptors that are modulated by cAMP-dependent signaling cascades in excitatory synapses.

Two chromatin-regulatory coactivators embedded in the cAMP signaling cascade, CREBBP and EP300, also carry documented ASD-related variation. Both genes encode histone acetyltransferase coactivators that integrate cAMP-responsive transcriptional programs at CREB-regulated promoters, and rare, potentially damaging variants in CREBBP, as well as its inclusion in ASD genetic surveys, link disruption of these transcriptional coactivators to autistic phenotypes.

Within the KEGG cAMP signaling pathway architecture, the enriched genes are concentrated in the signal transduction and effector segments rather than at the level of extracellular ligands. GNAI1 provides a proximal G protein node that modulates adenylyl cyclase activity and thus cAMP production. BRAF and PIK3R2 occupy downstream branches that connect cAMP signaling to ERK/MAPK and PI3K cascades, respectively, both of which are represented as explicit cross-talk routes to adjacent KEGG signaling maps. CAMK2A, CAMK2B and CAMK2D, together with GRIN1, GRIN2A and GRIN2B, form a contiguous synaptic Ca2+-dependent branch downstream of cAMP-regulated channels and G protein–coupled receptors, while CREBBP and EP300 sit at the nuclear transcriptional endpoint of this chain. The remaining intersection genes, including voltage-gated Ca2+ channel component CACNA1C, metabotropic receptor GABBR2, ion transporters ATP1A1, ATP1A3, ATP2B1 and SLC9A1, the scaffold-like kinase PAK1, and glutamate receptor subunits GRIA2 and GRIA3, are distributed across the membrane-excitability and downstream effector zones rather than forming a single linear segment, indicating that ASD-enriched genes touch multiple functional gene lists within the cAMP map instead of a single branch.

Functionally, one cluster consists of ionotropic glutamate receptor genes GRIN1, GRIN2A, GRIN2B, GRIA2 and GRIA3, which encode NMDA and AMPA receptor subunits central to excitatory synaptic transmission and Ca2+ influx that couples synaptic activity to cAMP- and Ca2+-sensitive kinases. A second cluster includes CAMK2A, CAMK2B and CAMK2D, which represent Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent kinases that decode Ca2+ transients generated by these receptors and by cAMP-modulated channels. A third, membrane excitability and ion homeostasis cluster is formed by CACNA1C, GABBR2, ATP1A1, ATP1A3, ATP2B1 and SLC9A1, which together shape neuronal membrane potential, Ca2+ extrusion and pH/Na+ balance in the context of cAMP-responsive signaling. A final intracellular signaling and nuclear effector cluster comprises GNAI1, BRAF, PIK3R2, PAK1, CREBBP and EP300, integrating G protein signaling, MAPK and PI3K cross-talk, cytoskeletal-regulatory kinase activity and cAMP-responsive chromatin remodeling into transcriptional outcomes relevant for neuronal differentiation and synaptic plasticity.

The enrichment of autism spectrum disorder genes in the cAMP signaling pathway indicates that a substantial fraction of ASD genetic risk converges on cAMP-regulated synaptic transmission and activity-dependent transcription. The principal driver genes are GRIN2B, CREBBP, EP300 and GRIA2, which each have direct ASD-related genetic or mechanistic evidence and sit at key synaptic and nuclear integration points of the pathway. Known biochemical interactions among intersection genes, including the coupling of NMDA receptor subunits such as GRIN2B to CAMK2 family kinases and the recruitment of CREBBP and EP300 into CREB-dependent transcriptional complexes, connect synaptic receptor perturbations to altered gene-expression programs. This pattern supports a model in which ASD-associated variation in cAMP-coupled receptors, Ca2+-dependent kinases and chromatin coactivators disrupts the translation of synaptic activity into long-term neuronal and circuit-level adaptations.

pathways.name: Chromatin organization
pathways.pathway_description: Chromatin organization
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: Chromatin organization pathways regulate how DNA is packaged and accessed, and their disruption can alter large gene expression programs relevant to neurodevelopmental timing, neuronal differentiation, and cortical circuit formation in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The cited ASD studies implicating chromatin regulators (e.g., CHD8, CREBBP, BAZ2B, ASH1L) support a model in which global transcriptional dysregulation, rather than single-gene effects, contributes to ASD pathology.
Intersection-gene interpretation: The intersection genes ACTB, ACTL6B, ARID1A, ARID1B, and ARID2 encode core structural and remodeling components of chromatin-associated complexes, suggesting that ASD risk may converge on ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling and actin-based nuclear architecture. ARID1B in particular is directly linked to ASD and neuropathology, indicating that perturbation of SWI/SNF (BAF) complex function can disrupt neuronal gene expression programs critical for social and cognitive development.
PubMed literature synthesis: ASD neuropathology and animal model work implicating ARID1B and CHD8, together with reports of CREBBP and ASH1L mutations in ASD cohorts, collectively support chromatin remodeling and histone modification as recurrent mechanistic themes in ASD. paragraphs: 45 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in Chromatin organization (REAC:R-HSA-4839726).

Within this chromatin organization pathway, CREBBP and EP300 encode histone acetyltransferases that function as transcriptional co‑activators, catalyzing lysine acetylation on histone tails within multiprotein complexes assembled on chromatin. In autism spectrum disorder, CREBBP variation has been reported in cohort-based genetic studies from Middle Eastern populations, in which rare damaging CREBBP alleles contributed to the burden of diagnosed ASD, and CREBBP has also emerged in in silico network analyses of placental molecular alterations in ASD, indicating that disruption of CREBBP‑mediated chromatin acetylation is repeatedly observed in affected individuals. Consistent with this, EP300, which often acts in the same acetylation reactions and complexes as CREBBP within this Reactome event hierarchy, is annotated here as a catalytic component that modifies histone substrates in successive steps of the chromatin remodeling chain, supporting the view that perturbation of histone acetylation is a recurrent feature in ASD-linked chromatin organization genes.

The lysine demethylases KDM5C and KDM6B act as additional catalytic regulators of histone marks within the chromatin organization pathway, removing methyl groups from distinct lysine residues and thereby altering transcriptional competence of target loci. In the Middle Eastern ASD genetic study, rare coding variants in both KDM5C and KDM6B were identified among affected individuals, providing direct human genetic support that disruption of histone demethylation contributes to ASD risk. Within the Reactome framework, KDM5C and KDM6B participate as enzymes in successive reactions that convert methylated histone substrates to less‑methylated products, which then feed forward into downstream chromatin states governed by other modifiers in this gene set, highlighting a mechanistic chain by which demethylase dysfunction could propagate broader chromatin dysregulation in ASD.

ASH1L is a histone methyltransferase that catalyzes methylation at specific lysine residues and is annotated in this pathway as a component of chromatin‑associated complexes that deposit activating marks on histone substrates. De novo disruptive ASH1L mutations have been identified in a Chinese ASD cohort, where they occur as sporadic, likely gene‑damaging events in affected probands, reinforcing its status as a monogenic contributor to ASD within the broader chromatin organization context. ASH1L‑mediated methylation acts upstream or in parallel to the demethylation reactions carried out by KDM5C and KDM6B, situating these ASD‑linked genes within an interconnected reaction chain of methylation and demethylation steps that specify chromatin states.

ACTB, which encodes cytoplasmic beta‑actin, contributes to chromatin organization in this pathway as a structural component of nuclear actin complexes that interact with chromatin‑remodeling assemblies, where it functions as a non‑catalytic subunit influencing nucleoprotein architecture. Network‑based biomarker analysis in ASD has implicated ACTB within molecular interaction gene lists enriched for ASD, indicating that perturbation of nuclear and cytoskeletal actin‑containing complexes may intersect with chromatin regulatory mechanisms. In the curated Reactome event, ACTB acts alongside chromatin remodelers and histone modifiers, placing this ASD‑implicated gene at the interface between structural nuclear organization and the enzymatic modification machinery represented by the other intersection genes.

The remaining genes enriched in Chromatin organization can be grouped into several functional clusters. A first cluster comprises ATP‑dependent chromatin remodelers and associated core subunits, including SMARCA2, SMARCA4, SMARCC2 and ACTL6B, as well as ARID1A, ARID1B and ARID2, which serve as components of remodeling complexes that use ATP hydrolysis to reposition nucleosomes and to alter chromatin accessibility across successive reactions in the pathway. A second cluster consists of histone methyltransferases and their cofactors, including DNMT3A, DOT1L, EHMT1, KMT2A, KMT2C, KMT5B, NSD1, NSD2, SETD1A, SETD1B, SETD2, KAT6A, KANSL1, WDR5 and TRRAP, which act predominantly as catalytic subunits or scaffold components in complexes that deposit or help recruit enzymes depositing methyl and acetyl marks on histone substrates. A third cluster includes additional demethylases and chromatin‑binding readers such as KDM2B, KDM3B, KDM5B, PHF2, PHF21A and PHF8, which participate as enzymes or recognition gene lists that interpret or erase specific histone modifications in sequential reactions following initial methyltransferase activity. A fourth cluster encompasses chromatin‑associated transcriptional regulators and scaffold proteins, including CHD3, CHD4, HCFC1, ELP2, NCOA1, HDAC8, MSL3, TBL1XR1 and NSD‑interacting components, which integrate acetylation and methylation states with transcriptional output, while the core histone H4 genes H4C3, H4C5 and H4C11 function as substrate proteins undergoing modification by the catalytic enzymes described above.

Chromatin organization contributes to autism spectrum disorder in this analysis through convergent disruption of histone acetylation and methylation dynamics, nucleosome remodeling and higher‑order chromatin structure. The principal driver genes are CREBBP, KDM5C and KDM6B, which have direct ASD genetic evidence and occupy catalytic positions in the Reactome chromatin organization event, together with ASH1L and ACTB as additional ASD‑linked components of the modification and structural machinery. Documented genetic involvement of CREBBP, KDM5C and KDM6B in ASD, combined with their roles in successive acetylation and demethylation reactions on shared histone substrates within this pathway, supports a model in which interacting chromatin modifiers and structural factors jointly shape the transcriptional landscape relevant to ASD neurodevelopment.

pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: This pathway captures the fundamental machinery for neurotransmission at chemical synapses, including presynaptic metabolism, vesicle release, and postsynaptic receptor activation, and its disruption is a central mechanistic route to ASD-related circuit dysfunction. Altered synaptic transmission can shift excitation–inhibition balance and impair information processing, consistent with many neurophysiological findings in ASD.
Intersection-gene interpretation: CACNA1A, CACNA1E, and CACNA2D3 encode subunits of voltage-gated calcium channels that control presynaptic calcium influx and thus neurotransmitter release probability, so their perturbation can broadly affect synaptic strength and timing in ASD. ALDH5A1 participates in GABA metabolism and ARHGEF9 regulates inhibitory synapse organization, indicating that both excitatory and inhibitory components of chemical synaptic transmission are represented in this ASD-enriched pathway.
PubMed literature synthesis: Genetic and meta-analytic studies implicating GABRB2, GABRB3, GRIN2B, GRIA2, and NBEA in ASD converge on disrupted GABAergic and glutamatergic synaptic transmission as a key disease mechanism. Neuropathology and animal model work further support that ASD-associated genes affecting ionotropic receptors and synaptic scaffolding act within the broader framework of chemical synaptic transmission represented by this pathway.
Cell/tissue context: The evidence supports involvement of cortical, limbic, and cerebellar synapses, particularly GABAergic and glutamatergic synapses in these brain regions, but does not resolve more specific cell types beyond these general neuronal populations.

paragraphs: 30 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in Transmission across Chemical Synapses (REAC:R-HSA-112315).

Among the enriched genes, GABRB3 and GABRB2 encode β subunits of the GABAA receptor, which acts as a ligand-gated chloride channel mediating fast inhibitory transmission at chemical synapses. A meta-analysis of GABRB3 gene polymorphisms and susceptibility to autism spectrum disorder reported a statistically significant association between specific GABRB3 variants and increased ASD risk, indicating that altered GABRB3 function contributes measurably to disease liability. GABRB2 has likewise been implicated in ASD in regional expression studies showing that ASD-associated genes, including GABRB2, are enriched in discrete cortical and cerebellar territories that are critical for social and cognitive function, supporting a role for inhibitory synapse components in ASD neuropathology.

GRIN2B and GRIA2 represent key glutamatergic receptor genes within this pathway. GRIN2B encodes an NMDA receptor subunit that forms part of a voltage- and ligand-gated cation channel essential for excitatory synaptic transmission and plasticity; neuropathological and animal-model work has directly linked GRIN2B disruption to ASD-related phenotypes, and independent genetic studies in distinct populations, including Vietnamese children, have identified GRIN2B variants in individuals with ASD. GRIA2 encodes an AMPA receptor subunit that mediates fast excitatory synaptic currents, and its inclusion among ASD-associated genes in population-specific genetic surveys of the Middle Eastern population further supports the clinical relevance of disturbed glutamatergic signaling in ASD.

NBEA, DLG4 and CASK illustrate how synaptic scaffolding and vesicle-associated genes embedded in Transmission across Chemical Synapses contribute to ASD risk. NBEA encodes a scaffolding protein enriched in synaptic and vesicular compartments; ASD gene-mapping studies that examined spatial gene expression reported that ASD-associated genes, including NBEA, concentrate in limbic, cortical and cerebellar regions, implicating NBEA-linked synaptic processes in these circuits. DLG4, a postsynaptic density scaffolding gene in this pathway, and CASK, a presynaptic scaffolding gene that has already appeared in earlier synaptic pathways in this report, both participate as components of multiprotein complexes that organize receptors and signaling enzymes at chemical synapses, providing a structural substrate through which receptor-level risk genes such as GRIN2B and GRIA2 can influence synaptic signaling.

The remaining functionally related genes in this pathway can be organized into clusters that together implement Transmission across Chemical Synapses. A receptor and transporter cluster includes GABRA3, GABBR2, GRIA3, GRIN1, GRIN2A, SLC6A1 and CACNA2D3, which encode subunits of inhibitory and excitatory neurotransmitter receptors, a GABA transporter and an auxiliary calcium channel component, acting as substrates or components of receptor and channel complexes that define synaptic input. An intracellular signaling cluster comprises CAMK2A, CAMK2B, CAMK2D, HRAS, RPS6KA3, GNAI1 and GNB2, which act as catalysts or G-protein subunits in postsynaptic signaling cascades downstream of receptor activation. A presynaptic vesicle release cluster, including RIMS1, SYT1, SYN1, VAMP2 and PPFIA3, encodes components of active zone scaffolds and SNARE-associated complexes that coordinate vesicle docking, calcium-sensing and fusion at presynaptic terminals. An additional metabolic and regulatory cluster contains ALDH5A1, CACNA1A, CACNA1E and NBEA, encompassing enzymes of neurotransmitter degradation, pore-forming calcium channel subunits and vesicular scaffolds that modulate the availability of transmitter and calcium influx needed for efficient synaptic transmission.

Transmission across Chemical Synapses thus contributes to autism spectrum disorder by concentrating genetic risk in receptor, signaling and vesicle-release mechanisms that operate sequentially within the same set of synaptic reactions. The principal driver genes are GABRB3, GRIN2B and GRIA2, which each have direct human genetic or clinical evidence linking variation to ASD and sit at critical excitatory–inhibitory receptor nodes in this pathway. Established interactions between DLG4 and NMDA receptor subunits such as GRIN1 and GRIN2A, as well as between RIMS1, SYT1, VAMP2 and other presynaptic components, place these risk genes in shared macromolecular complexes that execute single reaction steps in synaptic transmission rather than acting in isolation. Concentration of ASD-associated variants in both pre- and postsynaptic elements of this pathway supports a model in which perturbed coordination of neurotransmitter release and receptor-mediated signaling at chemical synapses is a central mechanism in ASD pathogenesis.

paragraphs: 92 submitted autism spectrum disorder-associated genes were significantly enriched in Gene expression (Transcription) (REAC:R-HSA-74160).

Several chromatin-modifying genes within this pathway represent well-established contributors to ASD risk through their roles in transcriptional regulation. EHMT1 encodes a histone methyltransferase that deposits repressive H3K9 methylation marks and regulates neuronal gene expression; pathogenic EHMT1 variants cause a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder with high rates of ASD diagnoses, and large clinical series report autistic features in a substantial fraction of affected individuals. DNMT3A encodes a DNA methyltransferase responsible for de novo cytosine methylation; loss-of-function DNMT3A variants underlie an overgrowth-intellectual disability syndrome in which ASD and autistic traits are frequent, indicating that disrupted establishment of DNA methylation patterns during development contributes to ASD-related phenotypes. KDM5B encodes a histone demethylase targeting H3K4 methylation, thereby shaping the activation state of promoters; recurrent disruptive KDM5B variants have been identified in ASD cohorts, supporting a role for misregulated promoter chromatin in ASD etiology.

Transcriptional co-activators CREBBP and EP300, which function as lysine acetyltransferases and scaffold proteins within large transcriptional complexes, further underscore the importance of acetylation-dependent control of gene expression in ASD. CREBBP has been repeatedly implicated in ASD genetics, including in population-specific studies where rare pathogenic variants or likely damaging missense changes were detected in ASD probands; one report of Middle Eastern ASD cases and an in silico analysis of placental transcriptomic data both highlight CREBBP among genes of interest. EP300, a close functional paralog of CREBBP that acetylates histones and numerous transcription factors, shares overlapping clinical phenotypes when mutated, including intellectual disability and autistic behaviors, suggesting that quantitative disturbance of histone acetylation and enhancer activity predisposes to ASD. KMT2A and KMT2C, two additional histone methyltransferases that catalyze H3K4 methylation at promoters and enhancers, participate in the same overarching chromatin-activation machinery and have been linked to neurodevelopmental syndromes in which ASD is commonly observed, aligning with a broader picture in which disruption of H3K4-regulated transcriptional programs confers ASD risk.

Glutamatergic signaling genes within this pathway connect transcriptional control directly to synaptic function. GRIN2B encodes an NMDA receptor subunit critical for excitatory synaptic transmission and plasticity; multiple independent ASD sequencing studies have repeatedly identified de novo loss-of-function and missense GRIN2B variants, and cohort descriptions document ASD diagnoses and severe language and cognitive impairments among carriers. GRIA2 encodes an AMPA receptor subunit shaping fast excitatory postsynaptic currents; rare deleterious GRIA2 variants were reported in ASD individuals in a genetic survey of Vietnamese children, again with prominent social-communication deficits. GRIN2A, another NMDA receptor subunit, similarly contributes to synaptic plasticity and language-related cortical circuits, and damaging variants in GRIN2A have been described in neurodevelopmental disorders with autistic traits, supporting the view that disturbance of glutamatergic receptor composition during development is a recurrent mechanism in ASD. Within the Gene expression (Transcription) pathway, these genes participate primarily as transcriptional targets and regulators of activity-dependent gene programs under the control of calcium-responsive transcription factors and chromatin modifiers rather than as classical catalysts.

Regulators of activity-dependent transcription and neuronal identity further strengthen the mechanistic bridge between transcriptional control and ASD phenotypes in this pathway. CAMK2A, CAMK2B and CAMK2D encode subunits of Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II, which acts as a serine/threonine kinase that phosphorylates transcriptional regulators in response to synaptic activity; damaging variants in CAMK2A and CAMK2B have been observed in individuals with ASD and intellectual disability, consistent with impaired coupling between synaptic signals and nuclear gene expression. MEF2C encodes a transcription factor that integrates calcium-dependent signaling with neuronal differentiation and synapse number; heterozygous MEF2C loss-of-function variants cause a recognizable neurodevelopmental syndrome with high prevalence of ASD diagnoses and severe language impairment. FOXG1, another transcription factor enriched here, specifies forebrain development and represses or activates distinct target gene sets; pathogenic FOXG1 variants produce a congenital variant of Rett-like encephalopathy in which autistic behaviors and impaired social interaction are prominent clinical features. In the Reactome hierarchy for Gene expression (Transcription), these genes act as catalysts or DNA-binding regulators in sub-pathways that translate neuronal activity into transcriptional responses across successive reaction steps.

Within the Reactome event structure, “Gene expression (Transcription)” serves as a higher-level pathway aggregating multiple sub-pathways such as transcription initiation, elongation, termination, chromatin modification, and mRNA maturation; it is nested under a broader parent event that encompasses gene expression and RNA processing. Intersection genes participate as catalysts of enzymatic modification, DNA-binding transcription factors, structural components of large multi-protein complexes, and substrates within successive reactions that convert chromatin templates into mature transcripts. For example, CREBBP and EP300 act as catalytic acetyltransferase subunits in co-activator complexes, while KMT2A, KMT2C, EHMT1, DNMT3A, and KDM5B serve as catalytic or regulatory components of histone and DNA methylation complexes that modify chromatin substrates. Transcription factors such as MEF2C, FOXG1, NR2F1, NFIB, NFIX, NR4A2 and MSX2 function as DNA-bound substrates and regulators whose activity or chromatin context is modified by these enzymes in sequential reactions, ultimately shaping transcriptional output relevant for neuronal development and function.

Beyond these key examples, the remaining enriched genes segregate into several functionally coherent transcriptional clusters. A first cluster comprises core components of chromatin remodeling and transcriptional co-regulator complexes, including ACTL6B, ARID1A, ARID1B, ARID2, CHD3, CHD4, KANSL1, KAT6A, and KDM5B, which cooperate in nucleosome repositioning and post-translational histone modification to modulate promoter and enhancer accessibility. A second cluster consists of general transcriptional machinery and Mediator-related genes, such as MED13, CCNK, CDK13, CDK8, CTR9, POLR3A, and INTS1, which act in transcription initiation, pause–release, and coupling of transcription to RNA processing. A third cluster includes mTOR pathway and phosphatase regulators, notably MTOR, PPP2CA, PPP2R5C, and PPM1D, which influence transcription indirectly by modulating kinase signaling cascades and the phosphorylation state of transcriptional regulators. A fourth cluster encompasses transcription factors and nuclear cofactors shaping neuronal and glial lineage identity, including NFIB, NFIX, NR2F1, NR4A2, MSX2, PAX5, LDB1 and HCFC1. A final cluster covers RNA processing and turnover machinery, including CPSF7, CNOT1, CNOT3, PSMD11, PSMD12, and NUP155, which participate in cleavage and polyadenylation, deadenylation-dependent mRNA decay, proteasomal regulation of transcription factors, and nucleocytoplasmic transport, thereby fine-tuning transcript availability downstream of initial transcriptional events.

The Gene expression (Transcription) pathway thus contributes to ASD by aggregating multiple layers of transcriptional and chromatin regulation with direct links to neurodevelopmental phenotypes. The principal driver genes are GRIN2B, CREBBP, GRIA2 and ACTB, all of which have been specifically highlighted in ASD-focused studies, with GRIN2B and GRIA2 connecting transcriptional regulation to excitatory synaptic function and CREBBP integrating chromatin acetylation with neuronal gene expression, while ACTB has emerged as a biomarker candidate in network-based analyses of ASD. Multiple documented and inferred interactions between intersection genes, such as the cooperative activity of CREBBP and EP300 within co-activator complexes and the functional interplay of KMT2A/KMT2C with KDM5B on H3K4 methylation states, indicate that combinatorial perturbation of these transcriptional gene lists can converge on ASD-relevant pathways. Disruption of this densely interconnected transcriptional architecture offers a coherent explanation for how diverse genetic lesions in chromatin regulators, transcription factors, and synaptic receptors converge on shared ASD phenotypes.

interpretation_points.label: Disease pathology and relevance
interpretation_points.text: This broad pathway encompasses transcriptional control of gene expression, and ASD genetics increasingly points to global dysregulation of transcriptional programs rather than a single signaling cascade. Disruption of transcriptional machinery can alter the expression of many neurodevelopmental and synaptic genes, providing a systems-level mechanism for ASD pathology.

interpretation_points.label: Intersection-gene interpretation
interpretation_points.text: ARID1A and ARID1B are SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling components whose disruption can broadly reprogram transcription, and ARID1B has direct ASD genetic support, implicating chromatin-based transcriptional control in ASD. ACTB, ACTL6B, and AGO2 contribute to cytoskeletal architecture, chromatin remodeling, and post-transcriptional regulation, respectively, indicating that both core transcriptional and RNA-regulatory processes intersect with ASD risk.

interpretation_points.label: PubMed literature synthesis
interpretation_points.text: ASD gene studies highlighting ARID1B and ACTB in genetic and biomarker analyses support a model in which altered chromatin remodeling and cytoskeletal-linked transcriptional regulation contribute to ASD. Additional ASD-associated transcriptional regulators (e.g., CREBBP, GRIN2B, GRIA2 from the attached literature) reinforce that widespread perturbation of gene expression programs is a recurrent theme in ASD etiology.
